description: Served from GitHub Pages. The app downloads this on launch; questions here replace local ones with the same id. Add questions to the list, or split into files and list them under "includes".

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with stage 4 CKD and heart failure is brought in with weakness. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was started 4 days ago; he also takes spironolactone and lisinopril. BP 104/62 mmHg. Rhythm strip shown.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate first treatment?
questions.explanation: Tall, narrow, peaked T waves with a widened QRS, flattened P waves, and a long PR indicate severe hyperkalemia with conduction toxicity (trimethoprim acts like amiloride, on top of an MRA and ACE inhibitor in CKD). The first step is IV calcium, which stabilizes the myocardial membrane within minutes. Shifting (insulin/dextrose, β-agonist) and removal (binders, diuretics, dialysis) follow immediately.

why_not.A: Binders act over hours and don't protect the heart now.
why_not.B: Insulin is the next step, but it takes 15–30 minutes to work and doesn't stabilize the membrane.
why_not.D: Dialysis may be needed, but arranging it takes time; protect the myocardium first.
why_not.E: Loop diuretics help removal later, if the kidneys respond.

questions.pearl: ECG changes of hyperkalemia → calcium first, then shift, then remove.
references: KDIGO 2020 Controversies Conference on Potassium
UK Kidney Association Hyperkalaemia Guideline 2023

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension is hypotensive on postoperative day 1 after hip replacement. She received furosemide overnight for “crackles” and has had poor oral intake. BP is 78/48 mmHg and heart rate 118/min. There is a new harsh grade 3/6 systolic murmur at the left sternal border that becomes louder when she is helped to sit upright. Bedside echocardiography shows a small, hyperdynamic left ventricle with concentric hypertrophy (septum 15 mm), systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve with posteriorly directed mitral regurgitation, and a late-peaking LVOT gradient of 90 mmHg.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: This is dynamic LVOT obstruction (SAM with a late-peaking “dagger” gradient) unmasked by hypovolemia, tachycardia, and catecholamine drive in a hypertrophied ventricle. The murmur grows with upright posture because preload falls. Treatment restores preload and afterload while slowing the heart: IV fluid plus a pure α-agonist (phenylephrine), followed by a β-blocker once perfusion is restored.

why_not.A: Inotropes increase contractility and narrow the outflow tract further, worsening the gradient.
why_not.B: An IABP lowers afterload during systole, which increases the LVOT gradient; it is contraindicated in dynamic LVOT obstruction.
why_not.C: Further diuresis reduces LV cavity size and worsens obstruction — likely how she got here.
why_not.D: Venodilation lowers preload and afterload, which increases the gradient and can cause collapse.

questions.pearl: When the murmur gets louder with standing/Valsalva and the patient is hypotensive, do the opposite of cardiogenic shock: fluids, phenylephrine, β-blocker — no inotropes, nitrates, or IABP.
references: 2024 AHA/ACC/AMSSM/HRS/PACES/SCMR Guideline for Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy

links.label: Wikipedia: Systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man reports 2 days of light-headedness and fatigue. He went camping in northern Wisconsin in June; 3 weeks ago he had a large, slowly expanding red patch on his thigh that faded without treatment. He has migratory arthralgias. BP 118/72 mmHg; he is alert. Rhythm strip shown.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Admission to telemetry, IV ceftriaxone, and temporary pacing if needed
options.C: Oral doxycycline for 21 days as an outpatient

questions.explanation: The strip shows complete heart block: regular P waves marching through, a regular narrow junctional escape, and no consistent PR relationship. In a young patient after an erythema migrans–like rash in an endemic area, this is Lyme carditis. Symptomatic patients, PR >300 ms, or second/third-degree block warrant hospitalization with continuous monitoring and IV ceftriaxone, switching to oral therapy once block improves (total 14–21 days). Use temporary pacing for hemodynamically significant bradycardia; the block usually resolves within days to weeks, so a permanent pacemaker should be avoided.

why_not.B: Lyme AV block is typically reversible; implanting a permanent device prematurely exposes him to lifelong device risks.
why_not.C: Oral therapy is appropriate for mild carditis (PR <300 ms, asymptomatic). High-grade block needs inpatient IV therapy and monitoring.
why_not.D: Atropine may not help infranodal block and does not treat the cause.
why_not.E: Glucocorticoids have no proven benefit and are not recommended.

questions.pearl: Young patient + high-grade AV block + tick exposure: think Lyme. Admit, IV ceftriaxone, temporary pace if needed — avoid a permanent pacemaker.
references: 2020 IDSA/AAN/ACR Lyme Disease Guidelines
CDC: Lyme carditis clinical guidance

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman has had two episodes of abrupt loss of consciousness without prodrome in the past month, one causing a facial laceration. She takes no AV-nodal–blocking drugs. Electrolytes, TSH, and troponin are normal; echocardiogram shows a normal LVEF. Telemetry strip shown.

diagrams.caption: Lead V1. Compare the PR intervals before and after each non-conducted P wave.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Observation, since this block is usually benign

questions.explanation: Regular P waves with a constant PR interval in conducted beats and an abrupt non-conducted P wave (no progressive PR prolongation) is Mobitz type II second-degree AV block. The wide QRS (RBBB pattern) places the block below the His bundle. Infranodal block is unstable and progresses to complete heart block, and with syncope and no reversible cause it's a class I indication for permanent pacing.

why_not.A: Wenckebach (Mobitz I) at the AV node is often benign; Mobitz II with a wide QRS isn't.
why_not.C: Atropine speeds the sinus rate and can worsen infranodal block by sending more impulses into diseased tissue.
why_not.D: EP study adds nothing when the surface ECG already shows infranodal block with symptoms.
why_not.E: Theophylline is used for some post-transplant or inferior-MI bradycardias, not structural infranodal disease.

questions.pearl: Constant PR then a dropped beat (Mobitz II), especially with a wide QRS = infranodal → pacemaker. Atropine can make it worse.
references: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man is found outdoors on a January morning, confused and shivering intermittently. Core (esophageal) temperature is 29.5°C; BP 96/58 mmHg; he has a pulse. Glucose 112 mg/dL, K⁺ 4.1 mEq/L. His ECG is shown.

diagrams.caption: Look at the junction between the QRS and the ST segment.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Prophylactic IV amiodarone for the ECG findings
options.C: Active rewarming (warm IV fluids, forced warm air), with gentle handling and continuous monitoring
options.D: Emergent cardiac catheterization for J-point elevation

questions.explanation: The prominent positive deflections at the J point (Osborn, or J, waves), sinus bradycardia, and prolonged PR and QT are classic for moderate hypothermia (28–32°C). Osborn waves shrink as the patient warms. Bradycardia here is physiologic and usually doesn't need pacing or atropine. Treat with active external and minimally invasive rewarming, gentle handling (rough movement can trigger VF), and monitoring. Below 28°C or with instability, ECMO/cardiopulmonary bypass rewarming is preferred.

why_not.A: Antiarrhythmics are ineffective in a cold heart, and the ECG changes resolve with warming.
why_not.B: Hypothermic bradycardia is appropriate for the lowered metabolic rate; pacing can provoke VF.
why_not.D: Osborn waves mimic ST elevation but reflect hypothermia, not acute coronary occlusion.
why_not.E: Atropine is generally ineffective for hypothermic bradycardia.

questions.pearl: Osborn (J) waves + bradycardia + long QT → hypothermia. Rewarm gently; don't pace or treat the ECG.
references: Paal P et al. Accidental hypothermia: 2021 update, Int J Environ Res Public Health 2022
Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for Hypothermia 2019
questions.image_query: Osborn J wave hypothermia ECG

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has her fourth episode of pleuritic chest pain in 14 months. The first episode followed a viral illness. Each recurrence has occurred when prednisone was tapered below 10 mg/day despite continuous colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily with confirmed adherence. Today: temperature 38.1°C, friction rub, diffuse ST elevation with PR depression, small effusion without tamponade physiology, CRP 64 mg/L. Tuberculosis testing, ANA, and pregnancy test are negative.
questions.question: In addition to continuing colchicine, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Increase prednisone to 1 mg/kg/day and taper over 4 weeks
options.E: Add warfarin to prevent pericardial adhesions

questions.explanation: She has recurrent, corticosteroid-dependent, colchicine-resistant pericarditis with an inflammatory phenotype (fever, elevated CRP). This autoinflammatory, IL-1–driven phenotype responds strikingly to IL-1 blockade (rilonacept in RHAPSODY; anakinra in AIRTRIP), which also allows glucocorticoid withdrawal. The 2025 ESC guideline endorses IL-1 antagonists for recurrent pericarditis refractory to colchicine and glucocorticoids.

why_not.B: High-dose glucocorticoids are associated with more recurrences and steroid dependence; low-to-moderate doses with slow tapers are preferred.
why_not.C: Pericardiectomy is a last resort for refractory recurrent pericarditis after medical options, including IL-1 blockade, have failed.
why_not.D: There is no tamponade or diagnostic uncertainty; the workup for secondary causes is negative.
why_not.E: Anticoagulation has no role in pericarditis and risks hemopericardium.

questions.pearl: Recurrent pericarditis with fever/high CRP, steroid-dependent despite colchicine → IL-1 blockade (rilonacept/anakinra) to get off steroids.
references: 2025 ESC Guidelines for Myocarditis and Pericarditis
Klein AL et al. RHAPSODY, NEJM 2021
Brucato A et al. AIRTRIP, JAMA 2016
questions.image_query: acute pericarditis ECG diffuse ST elevation PR depression

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma has 3 days of worsening dyspnea and light-headedness. BP 92/70 mmHg, HR 122/min, JVP to the angle of the jaw, clear lungs, and systolic BP falls by 18 mmHg on inspiration. His ECG is shown.

diagrams.caption: Note the voltage and how QRS amplitude changes from beat to beat.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: IV metoprolol to control the heart rate
options.D: CT pulmonary angiography before any intervention

questions.explanation: Sinus tachycardia, low QRS voltage, and electrical alternans (the heart swinging within a large effusion) with hypotension, distended neck veins, and pulsus paradoxus is cardiac tamponade, most likely malignant. Confirm with bedside echo (RA/RV diastolic collapse, plethoric IVC) and perform urgent pericardiocentesis. Support preload with fluids while preparing.

why_not.A: Diuresis lowers preload and can precipitate collapse in tamponade.
why_not.B: The tachycardia is compensatory; slowing it drops cardiac output.
why_not.D: PE can cause tachycardia and hypotension, but the ECG and pulsus point to tamponade, and the CT trip is dangerous in an unstable patient.
why_not.E: Anti-inflammatories treat pericarditis, not hemodynamic compromise from a large effusion.

questions.pearl: Low voltage + electrical alternans + tachycardia = big effusion swinging → echo and drain if hemodynamics are impaired. No diuretics or rate control.
references: 2025 ESC Guidelines for Myocarditis and Pericarditis
Spodick DH. Acute cardiac tamponade, NEJM 2003
questions.image_query: electrical alternans ECG pericardial effusion

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman on methadone maintenance received IV ondansetron and azithromycin for vomiting and bronchitis. She has had several brief episodes of light-headedness on telemetry. K⁺ 3.2 mEq/L, Mg²⁺ 1.4 mg/dL. One episode is shown; it terminated spontaneously after 9 seconds. She is now awake with BP 118/70 mmHg.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.explanation: A pause-dependent, markedly prolonged QT followed by polymorphic VT whose axis twists around the baseline is torsades de pointes, here from QT-prolonging drugs (methadone, ondansetron, azithromycin) plus hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. First-line therapy is IV magnesium sulfate 2 g, given even if serum Mg²⁺ is normal, together with stopping offending drugs and repleting potassium to high-normal. Recurrent, bradycardia-dependent runs respond to raising the heart rate (temporary overdrive pacing or isoproterenol).

why_not.A: Amiodarone prolongs the QT and can perpetuate torsades.
why_not.B: Procainamide (and its metabolite NAPA) prolongs the QT.
why_not.C: Synchronization is unreliable in polymorphic VT; sustained, unstable torsades gets unsynchronized defibrillation. She is stable and the run ended on its own.
why_not.E: Lidocaine has a minor role in refractory cases, but magnesium is first-line.

questions.pearl: Torsades: magnesium first; then stop QT drugs, K⁺ to 4.5–5, and speed the heart up (pacing/isoproterenol) if it recurs.
references: 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS Ventricular Arrhythmia Guideline
CredibleMeds.org QT drug lists

questions.stem: A 77-year-old man has HFpEF with two hospitalizations this year. History: bilateral carpal tunnel release, lumbar spinal stenosis surgery, and a spontaneous distal biceps tendon rupture. Echocardiogram: LV wall thickness 17 mm, LVEF 50%, global longitudinal strain with relative apical sparing. Technetium-99m pyrophosphate scan: grade 3 myocardial uptake (heart-to-contralateral ratio 1.8), confirmed on SPECT. His ECG is shown.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.D: Serum free light chain assay with serum and urine immunofixation
options.E: Begin vutrisiran after TTR gene sequencing

questions.explanation: Musculoskeletal red flags, low limb-lead voltage with a pseudo-infarct pattern despite LV thickening, apical-sparing strain, and grade 2–3 PYP uptake strongly suggest transthyretin (ATTR) cardiomyopathy. However, the non-biopsy diagnosis of ATTR is valid only if a monoclonal protein has been excluded — AL amyloid can also take up bone tracers, and AL is a hematologic emergency with completely different treatment. So the next step is serum FLC plus serum and urine immunofixation. If all three are negative, ATTR is diagnosed without biopsy, and TTR genotyping then distinguishes wild-type from variant disease.

why_not.A: Starting ATTR therapy before excluding AL risks missing a rapidly fatal, treatable plasma-cell disorder.
why_not.B: Biopsy is needed only if a monoclonal protein is found or imaging is equivocal.
why_not.C: Fat-pad aspirate has low sensitivity for ATTR (especially wild-type) and doesn't replace monoclonal protein screening.
why_not.E: Genotyping is appropriate after AL is excluded; it doesn't establish the amyloid type.

questions.pearl: Positive PYP is ATTR only after a negative FLC + serum IFE + urine IFE. Monoclonal protein present → tissue biopsy with typing.
references: Gillmore JD et al. Circulation 2016 (non-biopsy diagnosis)
2023 ACC Expert Consensus Decision Pathway on Cardiac Amyloidosis
questions.image_query: technetium pyrophosphate scan grade 3 cardiac uptake ATTR amyloidosis

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after his wife found him making gurgling, gasping sounds at 3 AM; he could not be roused for about 30 seconds, then recovered fully without confusion. He had a febrile viral illness last week, now resolved. His brother died suddenly in his sleep at age 38. He takes no medications and does not use drugs. Vital signs and examination are normal; he is afebrile. Electrolytes, troponin, and echocardiogram are normal. The ECG obtained on arrival is shown (right precordial leads placed in the standard 4th intercostal space).
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Exercise treadmill test to look for exercise-induced ventricular arrhythmia
options.C: Programmed electrical stimulation; ICD only if VF is inducible
options.D: Reassurance, aggressive antipyretic use with future fevers, and outpatient follow-up

questions.explanation: The ECG shows a spontaneous type 1 Brugada pattern: coved ST elevation ≥2 mm with a descending ST segment into an inverted T wave in V1–V2, recorded while afebrile and in standard lead position. Combined with a nocturnal episode with agonal respirations (an arrhythmic, not vasovagal, syncope) and a family history of sudden death, he has Brugada syndrome with presumed arrhythmic syncope. An ICD is recommended for patients with a spontaneous type 1 pattern and cardiac arrest, sustained VA, or recent syncope presumed due to VA. Fever control and avoidance of sodium-channel blockers remain important adjuncts but are not a substitute.

why_not.A: Brugada events cluster at rest and during sleep (high vagal tone); exercise testing does not risk-stratify this patient.
why_not.B: Class IC sodium-channel blockers (flecainide, ajmaline, procainamide) unmask and worsen the Brugada phenotype — they are diagnostic provocation agents, not therapy.
why_not.C: EP study is a weak tool used, if at all, for asymptomatic patients. A symptomatic patient with a spontaneous type 1 pattern needs an ICD regardless of inducibility.
why_not.D: Fever is a trigger, but the pattern is present while afebrile and he has had a probable arrhythmic event; avoidance strategies alone leave him at high risk of sudden death.

questions.pearl: Spontaneous type 1 Brugada + arrhythmic syncope = ICD. Sodium-channel blockers are the provocation test, not the treatment; quinidine is the drug option for storms or ICD refusal.
references: 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS Ventricular Arrhythmias & SCD Guideline
2022 ESC Guidelines for Ventricular Arrhythmias and Prevention of SCD
brugadadrugs.org
questions.image_query: type 1 Brugada pattern coved ST elevation V1 V2 ECG

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with hypertension has 2 weeks of palpitations and fatigue. BP 128/80 mmHg. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at exactly 150/min. During IV adenosine, the strip below is recorded.

diagrams.caption: Lead II during transient AV-nodal block from adenosine.

questions.question: After anticoagulation is addressed, which is the most effective long-term rhythm strategy?

options.C: Repeat adenosine whenever the tachycardia recurs

questions.explanation: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150/min should raise suspicion for atrial flutter with 2:1 block. Adenosine doesn't terminate flutter, but transient AV block unmasks the negative sawtooth flutter waves at ~300/min in the inferior leads: typical (cavotricuspid isthmus–dependent) flutter. CTI ablation succeeds in >90% and is first-line for symptomatic or recurrent typical flutter. Anticoagulation follows the same CHA₂DS₂-VASc rules as AF (his score is ≥1 for hypertension, and anticoagulation is generally recommended at ≥2 in men).

why_not.A: Antiarrhythmic drugs have lower efficacy and long-term toxicity compared with ablation for typical flutter.
why_not.C: Adenosine is diagnostic here, not therapeutic.
why_not.D: Rate control is difficult in flutter, and digoxin alone is ineffective, especially with exertion.
why_not.E: There's no pre-excitation; the circuit is in the right atrium.

questions.pearl: Regular narrow tachycardia at 150 = flutter 2:1 until proven otherwise. Adenosine unmasks the sawtooth; CTI ablation cures it.
references: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Atrial Fibrillation Guideline
2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT Guideline (atrial flutter)
questions.image_query: atrial flutter sawtooth flutter waves adenosine unmasking

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man had sudden left-hand weakness and dysarthria. MRI shows a 2.5-cm cortical infarct in the right MCA territory. CTA head/neck is normal. TTE with bubble study shows a large right-to-left shunt; TEE confirms a patent foramen ovale with an atrial septal aneurysm and no thrombus. A 30-day ambulatory monitor shows no atrial fibrillation. LDL 98 mg/dL, HbA1c 5.3%, no hypertension, no tobacco. Lower-extremity duplex is negative.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate secondary prevention strategy?

options.D: Percutaneous PFO closure plus antiplatelet therapy
options.E: Implantable loop recorder; defer other decisions until AF is excluded at 3 years

questions.explanation: He fits the population that benefited in CLOSE, REDUCE, and RESPECT: age 18–60, a nonlacunar embolic-appearing infarct, no competing mechanism after thorough evaluation, and a high-risk PFO (atrial septal aneurysm and large shunt; RoPE score high). In such patients PFO closure plus antiplatelet therapy reduces recurrent stroke compared with antiplatelet therapy alone.

why_not.A: Antiplatelet therapy alone was inferior to closure in this high-risk-PFO population.
why_not.B: DOACs (NAVIGATE-ESUS, RE-SPECT ESUS) did not beat aspirin in ESUS overall, and anticoagulation is not preferred over closure here.
why_not.C: Anticoagulation is reasonable for patients who decline closure or who have a separate indication, but it carries bleeding risk and is not the preferred strategy.
why_not.E: He is young, without AF risk factors, and has already had 30 days of monitoring; delaying closure leaves recurrence risk untreated.

questions.pearl: Age ≤60, embolic-appearing stroke, high-risk PFO (ASA or large shunt), and no other cause → closure + antiplatelet.
references: 2021 AHA/ASA Secondary Stroke Prevention Guideline
AAN 2020 Practice Advisory Update on PFO
Mas JL et al. CLOSE, NEJM 2017

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man has had 2 hours of rapid palpitations. He is alert, BP 112/70 mmHg, and has no chest pain. Rhythm strip shown.

diagrams.caption: Lead II. Note rate, regularity, and the beat-to-beat variation in QRS width and upstroke.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: An irregularly irregular, very fast (>200/min), wide-complex rhythm with varying QRS morphology and slurred upstrokes is atrial fibrillation conducting over an accessory pathway. Blocking the AV node removes the competing route and lets more impulses traverse the pathway, which can degenerate into VF. In a stable patient, use a drug that slows pathway conduction — IV procainamide or ibutilide; if unstable, synchronized cardioversion. Definitive therapy is accessory-pathway ablation.

why_not.A: Adenosine blocks the AV node and can precipitate VF; it may also provoke more AF.
why_not.B: Nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers are potentially harmful in pre-excited AF.
why_not.C: β-Blockers likewise favor conduction down the pathway and are listed as potentially harmful.
why_not.D: Digoxin shortens accessory-pathway refractoriness and is contraindicated.

questions.pearl: Fast, irregular, and wide with shifting QRS shapes = pre-excited AF. No AV-nodal blockers (and no IV amiodarone per US guidelines); procainamide/ibutilide or shock.
references: 2014 AHA/ACC/HRS AF Guideline (Class III: harm for IV amiodarone, adenosine, digoxin, nondihydropyridine CCB)
2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT Guideline
2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF Guideline
questions.image_query: pre-excited atrial fibrillation WPW ECG irregular wide complex tachycardia

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman, 5 weeks postpartum, has 2 hours of chest pressure. She has no cardiovascular risk factors. Troponin peaks at 3.1 ng/mL; ECG shows T-wave inversions in V2–V4. Coronary angiography shows a long, smooth, diffuse narrowing of the mid-to-distal LAD that tapers abruptly from normal caliber, with TIMI 3 flow; the other arteries are normal and free of plaque. Her pain has resolved and she is hemodynamically stable.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: PCI with a long drug-eluting stent
options.B: Conservative management with a β-blocker and inpatient monitoring, plus imaging to screen for fibromuscular dysplasia

questions.explanation: A young peripartum woman without atherosclerosis whose angiogram shows a long, smooth, tapering lesion has spontaneous coronary artery dissection (type 2 angiographic pattern: intramural hematoma). Most dissections heal spontaneously within weeks, and PCI has high complication rates (propagating the dissection, hematoma extension), so stable patients with preserved flow are treated conservatively with a β-blocker and several days of inpatient monitoring. SCAD is strongly associated with fibromuscular dysplasia, so screen once with head-to-pelvis CTA or MRA.

why_not.A: Stenting is reserved for ongoing ischemia, hemodynamic instability, or left main/proximal two-vessel dissection; here it risks iatrogenic propagation.
why_not.C: CABG is for left-main involvement or failed PCI in unstable patients, and grafts often fail as the native vessel heals.
why_not.D: Fibrinolysis can extend the intramural hematoma and is contraindicated.
why_not.E: There is no thrombus to treat; anticoagulation may expand the hematoma.

questions.pearl: Young woman, peripartum or emotional stressor, smooth tapering coronary lesion → SCAD: stable means conservative care with a β-blocker, plus screening for FMD.
references: Hayes SN et al. AHA Scientific Statement on SCAD, Circulation 2018
ESC ACVC position paper on SCAD 2018
questions.image_query: spontaneous coronary artery dissection type 2 angiogram tapering LAD

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has 18 months of progressive abdominal swelling and leg edema. He received mediastinal radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma at age 30. JVP is 16 cm and rises with inspiration; there is ascites. Echocardiogram: LVEF 60%, normal wall thickness, mild biatrial enlargement, an abrupt septal shift in early diastole, 30% respiratory variation in mitral E velocity, medial e′ 13 cm/s and lateral e′ 9 cm/s. NT-proBNP 210 pg/mL. CRP is normal, and cardiac MRI shows a thickened pericardium without late gadolinium enhancement. Right and left heart catheterization (simultaneous ventricular pressures, with respiration) is shown.

diagrams.caption: Simultaneous LV and RV pressure. Note the early diastolic dip followed by a plateau, equal diastolic pressures, and how the systolic peaks change in each ventricle during inspiration.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive therapy?

options.C: Anti-inflammatory therapy with colchicine and an NSAID for 3 months, then reassess

questions.explanation: Radiation can cause either constriction or restrictive cardiomyopathy; the data separate them. The tracing shows ventricular interdependence: during inspiration RV systolic pressure rises while LV systolic pressure falls (discordance, i.e., a high systolic area index), plus equalized diastolic pressures with a dip-and-plateau. The echo supports constriction — septal bounce, >25% mitral inflow variation, and preserved (even higher medial than lateral, “annulus reversus”) e′ — and the modest NT-proBNP fits constriction more than restriction. With normal CRP and no pericardial LGE, this is chronic, non-inflammatory constriction, which requires pericardiectomy. (Radiation-associated constriction carries higher surgical mortality and worse long-term survival than idiopathic disease, which is worth counseling about, but it is still the definitive therapy.)

why_not.B: Transplant is for restrictive cardiomyopathy or end-stage myocardial disease. Concordant ventricular pressures and low e′ would point that way; this patient has discordance and preserved e′.
why_not.C: A trial of anti-inflammatories is appropriate for transient/inflammatory constriction (elevated CRP, pericardial LGE, recent onset). Here inflammation markers are absent and symptoms are chronic.
why_not.D: Balloon pericardiotomy treats recurrent effusions, not a thickened constricting pericardium.
why_not.E: ATTR amyloid is a restrictive cardiomyopathy with low e′, increased wall thickness, and elevated NT-proBNP — none present here.

questions.pearl: Constriction: discordant LV/RV systolic peaks with respiration, e′ preserved (annulus reversus), modest BNP. Restriction: concordant peaks, low e′, high BNP.
references: 2025 ESC Guidelines for Myocarditis and Pericarditis
Talreja DR et al. J Am Coll Cardiol 2008 (systolic area index)
Welch TD et al. Circ Cardiovasc Imaging 2014 (Mayo echo criteria)

questions.stem:
A 79-year-old man has NYHA class III dyspnea despite guideline-directed therapy for ischemic cardiomyopathy. Resting transthoracic echo and low-dose dobutamine stress echo results are shown.
RestPeak dobutamine
LVEF30%38%
Stroke volume index29 mL/m²37 mL/m² (+28%)
Mean AV gradient24 mmHg45 mmHg
Aortic valve area0.8 cm²0.85 cm²
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Continue medical therapy; the valve is only moderately stenotic
options.B: CT aortic valve calcium scoring before any decision
options.C: Balloon aortic valvuloplasty as definitive therapy
options.E: Cardiac resynchronization therapy and repeat echo in 6 months

questions.explanation: This is classic low-flow, low-gradient AS with reduced EF. Dobutamine shows contractile (flow) reserve (SV rise ≥20%), and with higher flow the mean gradient reaches ≥40 mmHg while the AVA stays ≤1.0 cm². That defines true severe AS (stage D2), and symptomatic severe AS is an indication for AVR (TAVR is the usual choice at his age). In pseudo-severe AS, by contrast, the valve opens further with increased flow (AVA rises above 1.0 cm²) and the gradient stays low.

why_not.A: The resting gradient underestimates severity because flow is low; the stress study proves true severe stenosis.
why_not.B: CT calcium scoring is the tiebreaker when dobutamine is nondiagnostic (no flow reserve) or in paradoxical low-flow AS with preserved EF. This study is diagnostic.
why_not.C: Valvuloplasty is at most a bridge to definitive AVR; restenosis is rapid.
why_not.E: Delaying relief of a fixed severe obstruction in a symptomatic patient increases mortality; CRT does not address the valve.

questions.pearl: LF-LG AS with low EF: dobutamine → if SV rises ≥20% and the gradient reaches ≥40 with AVA ≤1.0 = true severe → AVR. If no flow reserve → CT calcium score.
references: 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for Valvular Heart Disease

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with asthma since childhood has had 3 exacerbations this year despite high-dose ICS–LABA. She coughs up brownish-black mucus plugs. Blood eosinophils 1,150/µL. Total IgE 2,800 IU/mL; Aspergillus fumigatus–specific IgE is elevated. ANCA is negative. HRCT shows central (proximal) bronchiectasis in the upper lobes with mucus plugs that are denser than the paraspinal muscle. She has no neuropathy, sinus disease, or rash.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Asthma with markedly elevated total IgE (≥500 IU/mL in the 2024 ISHAM criteria; here 2,800), Aspergillus-specific IgE, eosinophilia, central bronchiectasis, and high-attenuation mucus (pathognomonic when present) is ABPA. Treatment is oral glucocorticoids or itraconazole to reduce exacerbations and prevent progressive bronchiectasis, monitoring total IgE as a marker of activity.

why_not.B: EGPA features vasculitis (neuropathy, purpura, cardiac or renal involvement), sinus disease, and often MPO-ANCA; it does not cause central bronchiectasis with high-attenuation mucus.
why_not.C: Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia gives peripheral consolidation (the “photographic negative of pulmonary edema”) and often BAL eosinophilia >25%, without IgE >1,000 or bronchiectasis.
why_not.D: Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis presents with cavities, pleural thickening, or aspergillomas and positive Aspergillus IgG in patients with prior lung damage.
why_not.E: Löffler syndrome is transient migratory infiltrates, often from helminth larval migration, resolving within weeks.

questions.pearl: Asthma + total IgE ≥500 (2024 ISHAM; classically >1,000) + Aspergillus IgE + central bronchiectasis/high-attenuation mucus = ABPA.
references: ISHAM-ABPA working group revised clinical practice guidelines, Eur Respir J 2024
questions.image_query: ABPA CT central bronchiectasis high attenuation mucus finger in glove

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with influenza is intubated for hypoxemic respiratory failure. Bilateral opacities are present and there's no evidence of heart failure. Twelve hours later, on volume control (6 mL/kg predicted body weight), PEEP 14 cm H₂O, FiO₂ 0.8: PaO₂ 70 mmHg, plateau pressure 27 cm H₂O. He is deeply sedated and synchronous with the ventilator. MAP is 72 mmHg on low-dose norepinephrine.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Prone positioning for at least 16 hours per day
options.D: Stepwise recruitment maneuvers with PEEP titrated to best compliance

questions.explanation: He has severe ARDS (P/F 88 on PEEP ≥5) despite lung-protective ventilation. Prone positioning for ≥16 h/day, started early, reduced mortality in PROSEVA for P/F <150 and is strongly recommended.

why_not.A: HFOV increased mortality (OSCILLATE) and is not recommended.
why_not.C: Inhaled NO transiently improves oxygenation without a survival benefit; it is a rescue bridge at most.
why_not.D: Prolonged aggressive recruitment maneuvers with PEEP titration increased mortality in the ART trial.
why_not.E: ECMO is considered for refractory hypoxemia after proning and optimized ventilation (EOLIA criteria); it's not the next step before proning.

questions.pearl: Severe ARDS: low VT, plateau ≤30, then prone early (P/F <150). Avoid HFOV and aggressive recruitment.
references: Guérin C et al. PROSEVA, NEJM 2013
ATS/ESICM/SCCM 2024 ARDS Guideline Update
questions.image_query: prone positioning ARDS ICU

questions.stem: A 67-year-old former smoker with COPD (post-bronchodilator FEV₁ 52% predicted) takes tiotropium–olodaterol daily with good adherence and inhaler technique. He had two exacerbations requiring oral prednisone in the past year and no hospitalizations. Blood eosinophil count is 320/µL. He has no history of pneumonia or mycobacterial infection. He has no chronic sputum production.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his maintenance therapy?
questions.explanation: With recurrent exacerbations on LABA+LAMA and blood eosinophils ≥100/µL (and especially ≥300/µL), GOLD recommends escalating to LABA+LAMA+ICS. Single-inhaler triple therapy reduced exacerbations and, in IMPACT and ETHOS, all-cause mortality.

why_not.A: Roflumilast is for patients with chronic bronchitis and FEV₁ <50%, typically when eosinophils are low or exacerbations continue on triple therapy.
why_not.B: Azithromycin is an option in former smokers who keep exacerbating, usually after or instead of ICS when eosinophils are low; it carries QT and resistance concerns.
why_not.C: Dupilumab is for patients who continue to exacerbate on triple therapy with eosinophils ≥300/µL and a chronic bronchitis phenotype (BOREAS/NOTUS).
why_not.D: Dropping the LAMA removes a bronchodilator; LABA+ICS without LAMA is not recommended in COPD.

questions.pearl: Exacerbating on LABA/LAMA: eos ≥100 → add ICS; eos <100 → roflumilast (chronic bronchitis + FEV₁ <50%) or azithromycin.
references: GOLD 2025 Report
Lipson DA et al. IMPACT, NEJM 2018
Bhatt SP et al. NOTUS, NEJM 2024
questions.image_query: GOLD COPD follow-up pharmacological treatment algorithm eosinophils

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has 6 months of cough and exertional dyspnea that improve during a 2-week beach vacation and worsen on return home. She keeps six budgerigars in her living room and sleeps with a down comforter. HRCT shows ground-glass opacities, ill-defined centrilobular nodules, and lobular areas of decreased attenuation that become more conspicuous on expiratory images. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows 52% lymphocytes. There is no honeycombing.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most important intervention?

options.B: Complete avoidance of the inciting antigen
options.D: Mycophenolate mofetil started immediately in place of exposure changes

questions.explanation: Exposure to avian antigens, improvement away from home, centrilobular nodules with ground-glass and air trapping (the “three-density” pattern), and BAL lymphocytosis point to non-fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis. The cornerstone of treatment, and the best predictor of outcome, is antigen identification and complete avoidance (remove birds, feathers, and down bedding, and remediate the home). Glucocorticoids are added for severe or persistent disease.

why_not.A: Steroids may be used for significant impairment but don't replace avoidance, and long-term use has substantial toxicity.
why_not.C: Antifibrotics are for progressive fibrotic ILD despite management, not non-fibrotic HP.
why_not.D: Mycophenolate is a steroid-sparing option for fibrotic or refractory HP, never a substitute for removing the antigen.
why_not.E: There's no fibrosis; prognosis with avoidance is good.

questions.pearl: Better on vacation + birds/mold/hot tub + centrilobular nodules + air trapping + BAL lymphs >30–40% = HP. Remove the antigen first.
references: ATS/JRS/ALAT 2020 Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis Guideline
CHEST 2021 HP Guideline
questions.image_query: hypersensitivity pneumonitis CT three density sign centrilobular nodules

questions.stem: A 69-year-old retired accountant has 2 years of progressive dyspnea and dry cough. There are bibasilar “Velcro” crackles and clubbing. He takes no medications, has no birds, mold, or occupational exposures, and has no rash, joint, or muscle symptoms. ANA, RF, anti-CCP, and a myositis panel are negative. HRCT shows subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, without ground-glass, nodules, or air trapping. FVC is 68% predicted; DLCO is 45%. A multidisciplinary discussion agrees on the diagnosis.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Surgical lung biopsy to confirm the diagnosis

questions.explanation: A typical UIP pattern on HRCT in the right clinical context, with no exposures or connective tissue disease, establishes IPF without biopsy. Antifibrotics (nintedanib or pirfenidone) slow FVC decline. He should also get pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen assessment, vaccines, GERD evaluation if symptomatic, and early transplant referral.

why_not.A: Biopsy adds risk (acute exacerbation) and isn't needed when HRCT shows typical UIP with a consistent clinical context.
why_not.B: This triple therapy increased mortality and hospitalization in IPF (PANTHER-IPF) and is contraindicated.
why_not.D: Immunosuppression helps CTD-ILD and fibrotic HP, not IPF.
why_not.E: BAL is useful when HRCT is indeterminate or HP is suspected; it's unnecessary with typical UIP and no exposures.

questions.pearl: Typical UIP on HRCT + no alternative cause = IPF: no biopsy, no steroids, antifibrotic.
references: ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT 2022 IPF and Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis Guideline
Raghu G et al. PANTHER-IPF, NEJM 2012
questions.image_query: usual interstitial pneumonia HRCT honeycombing subpleural basal

questions.stem:
Twenty minutes after a transesophageal echocardiogram, a 31-year-old woman becomes dyspneic and cyanotic. Pulse oximetry reads 85% and doesn't improve with a non-rebreather mask. Arterial blood is chocolate-brown. She is alert; BP 122/76 mmHg. She has no history of G6PD deficiency. ABG and co-oximetry are shown.
TestResultReference
pH / PaCO₂7.43 / 36 mmHg
PaO₂ (FiO₂ ~0.9)412 mmHg
Methemoglobin34%<1.5%
Carboxyhemoglobin1%<2% (nonsmoker)
Lactate1.6 mmol/L<2.0
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.E: Oral ascorbic acid as sole therapy

questions.explanation: A saturation gap (normal PaO₂, low SpO₂ hovering around 85% regardless of FiO₂), chocolate-colored blood, and recent exposure to topical benzocaine (used for TEE) indicate acquired methemoglobinemia, confirmed by co-oximetry. A symptomatic patient or a level >20–30% calls for IV methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg, which uses NADPH-methemoglobin reductase to reduce Fe³⁺ back to Fe²⁺.

why_not.A: Hyperbaric oxygen treats carbon monoxide poisoning, where the carboxyhemoglobin fraction (not methemoglobin) is elevated.
why_not.B: Hydroxocobalamin is the antidote for cyanide.
why_not.C: Exchange transfusion is a rescue option when methylene blue fails or is contraindicated (e.g., G6PD deficiency).
why_not.E: Ascorbic acid acts slowly; it's an adjunct or an alternative only when methylene blue can't be used.

questions.pearl: SpO₂ stuck near 85% with a high PaO₂ = methemoglobinemia (benzocaine, dapsone, nitrites). Treat with methylene blue — unless G6PD deficient.
references: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.
FDA Drug Safety Communication on benzocaine 2018
questions.image_query: methemoglobinemia chocolate brown blood

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has 2 days of dyspnea after a long flight. BP 128/82 mmHg, HR 106/min, SpO₂ 93% on 2 L. CT pulmonary angiography shows bilateral main pulmonary artery emboli with an RV/LV diameter ratio of 1.3. High-sensitivity troponin T is elevated and NT-proBNP is 2,400 pg/mL. Hemoglobin and platelets are normal; she has no bleeding risk factors.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Parenteral anticoagulation with close monitoring for hemodynamic decompensation

questions.explanation: She is normotensive with both RV dysfunction on imaging and positive biomarkers, which makes her intermediate-high risk. Here systemic thrombolysis prevented hemodynamic decompensation but caused excess major and intracranial bleeding without reducing mortality (PEITHO). Standard therapy is anticoagulation (LMWH or UFH) with monitoring, with rescue reperfusion if she decompensates.

why_not.B: Full-dose thrombolysis is for high-risk (shock/hypotension) PE or for rescue after decompensation.
why_not.C: Filters are for patients who cannot be anticoagulated or who have recurrent PE despite adequate anticoagulation.
why_not.D: Embolectomy is reserved for high-risk PE when thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed.
why_not.E: RV strain with positive biomarkers excludes early discharge.

questions.pearl: Normotensive PE + RV strain + troponin = intermediate-high: anticoagulate and watch closely; lyse only for decompensation.
references: 2019 ESC Acute PE Guideline
Meyer G et al. PEITHO, NEJM 2014
questions.image_query: CT pulmonary angiogram saddle embolus RV dilation

questions.topic: Central sleep apnea in heart failure
questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 30%, NYHA class II) on optimized guideline-directed therapy reports fragmented sleep and daytime fatigue. His wife describes cycles of waxing and waning breathing with pauses during sleep. Polysomnography shows an apnea–hypopnea index of 38/h; 85% of events are central, in a crescendo–decrescendo (Cheyne–Stokes) pattern.
questions.question: Which of the following treatments should be avoided in this patient?

options.E: Further optimization of heart failure therapy, including evaluation for CRT

questions.explanation: He has central sleep apnea with Cheyne–Stokes respiration in HFrEF. In SERVE-HF, adaptive servo-ventilation increased all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in patients with LVEF ≤45% and predominantly central apnea, so ASV is contraindicated in this group. Treatment starts with optimizing heart failure therapy; CPAP, nocturnal oxygen, and phrenic nerve stimulation are accepted options.

why_not.A: CPAP can suppress central events and improve oxygenation (CANPAP), and it's an acceptable option.
why_not.B: Low-flow nocturnal oxygen reduces central apneas and is an accepted therapy.
why_not.D: Transvenous phrenic nerve stimulation (remedē system) is approved for moderate-severe CSA and is reasonable.
why_not.E: Improving cardiac function (including CRT when indicated) is first-line for CSA in heart failure.

questions.pearl: Cheyne–Stokes CSA with LVEF ≤45%: no ASV (SERVE-HF mortality signal).
references: Cowie MR et al. SERVE-HF, NEJM 2015
AASM 2016 Updated CSA Treatment Guideline
2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF Guideline (Class 3: Harm for ASV)
questions.image_query: Cheyne-Stokes respiration polysomnography crescendo decrescendo

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with severe asthma is intubated for hypercapnic respiratory failure. Settings: volume control, tidal volume 8 mL/kg, rate 30/min, inspiratory flow 60 L/min, PEEP 5 cm H₂O. Ten minutes later BP falls to 72/40 mmHg and HR rises to 128/min. Breath sounds are equal bilaterally and the trachea is midline. Peak pressure is 52 cm H₂O, plateau pressure 34 cm H₂O, and an end-expiratory hold shows a total PEEP of 18 cm H₂O. The ventilator flow–time waveform is shown.

diagrams.caption: Inspiratory flow is above zero; expiratory flow below. Look at where each expiration ends.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.B: Increase the respiratory rate to correct hypercapnia
options.C: Increase set PEEP to 15 cm H₂O
options.D: Briefly disconnect the patient from the ventilator, then reduce the rate and tidal volume to lengthen expiratory time
options.E: Start a norepinephrine infusion without changing ventilator settings

questions.explanation: Expiratory flow never returns to zero before the next breath, and the end-expiratory hold reveals intrinsic PEEP of ~13 cm H₂O above the set PEEP. Dynamic hyperinflation raises intrathoracic pressure, impedes venous return, and causes hypotension. The immediate fix is to disconnect the circuit for 30–60 seconds to let trapped gas escape, then lower minute ventilation (rate and/or tidal volume) and shorten inspiratory time to lengthen expiration, accepting permissive hypercapnia.

why_not.A: Equal breath sounds, a midline trachea, and the waveform point to auto-PEEP, not tension pneumothorax. If hypotension doesn't improve with disconnection, then consider pneumothorax.
why_not.B: A higher rate shortens expiratory time and worsens air trapping.
why_not.C: In a passive patient, set PEEP above roughly 80% of the intrinsic PEEP (here ~13 cm H₂O) adds to end-expiratory volume and worsens hyperinflation and hypotension.
why_not.E: Vasopressors don't address the mechanical cause; the hemodynamic collapse will recur.

questions.pearl: Ventilated asthmatic + hypotension: disconnect first. Then low rate, low VT, fast inspiratory flow, long expiration, permissive hypercapnia.
references: Leatherman J. Mechanical ventilation for severe asthma, Chest 2015
questions.image_query: auto-PEEP ventilator flow time waveform expiratory flow does not return to zero

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman has 4 months of exertional dyspnea and noisy breathing when she exerts herself. History: endotracheal intubation for 9 days for influenza pneumonia 2 years ago; total thyroidectomy for a large multinodular goiter 5 months ago; 25 pack-year smoking history. Her voice is weak and breathy. Lungs are clear at rest. FEV₁/FVC is 0.81. Her flow-volume loop is shown.

diagrams.caption: Patient loop (solid) with predicted normal (dashed). Expiratory flow is above the axis, inspiratory flow below.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation: The loop shows a flattened inspiratory limb with a preserved expiratory limb: a variable extrathoracic obstruction. During forced inspiration, negative intraluminal pressure collapses a floppy or narrowed extrathoracic airway; during expiration, positive pressure stents it open. With a breathy voice after thyroidectomy, bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury with vocal cord paralysis is the cause.

why_not.B: A rigid scar narrows the airway equally in both phases, giving a fixed obstruction: both limbs are flattened into a box shape. That was the trap in this history.
why_not.C: Intrathoracic lesions collapse during forced expiration (positive pleural pressure), flattening the expiratory limb instead.
why_not.D: COPD gives a scooped (concave) expiratory limb with a reduced FEV₁/FVC; her ratio is normal.
why_not.E: Restriction produces a small, narrow loop with normal shape, shifted toward lower volumes.

questions.pearl: Flat inspiration = variable extrathoracic (vocal cords). Flat expiration = variable intrathoracic (tracheomalacia, intrathoracic tumor). Both flat = fixed (stenosis).
references: ATS/ERS 2005 Interpretive Strategies for Lung Function Tests
Stanojevic S et al. ERS/ATS technical standard on interpretive strategies 2022
questions.image_query: flow volume loop variable extrathoracic obstruction fixed obstruction comparison

questions.stem:
A 74-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 25%) has a right pleural effusion. His furosemide dose was doubled 5 days ago for weight gain, and he has lost 4 kg. Thoracentesis yields 900 mL of straw-colored fluid.
TestResultReference
Pleural protein / serum protein3.4 / 6.2 g/dLratio ≤0.5
Pleural LDH / serum LDH168 / 210 U/Lratio ≤0.6; serum ULN 222
Pleural albumin / serum albumin1.9 / 3.5 g/dL
Pleural nucleated cells640/µL (78% lymphocytes)
Pleural NT-proBNP4,800 pg/mL
Pleural glucose / pH118 mg/dL / 7.46
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: CT chest with contrast followed by thoracoscopic pleural biopsy
options.B: Attribute the effusion to heart failure and continue optimizing heart failure therapy
options.D: Repeat thoracentesis for cytology on two more occasions

questions.explanation: By Light's criteria the fluid looks exudative (protein ratio 0.55, LDH ratio 0.80, pleural LDH >⅔ ULN), but diuresis concentrates pleural protein and LDH, so ~25% of heart-failure transudates are misclassified. When the clinical picture says transudate, check the serum–pleural albumin gradient (>1.2 g/dL = transudate; here 1.6) or the protein gradient (>3.1 g/dL), and/or pleural NT-proBNP (>1,500 pg/mL strongly supports heart failure). This effusion is due to heart failure, and no invasive workup is needed.

why_not.A: Biopsy is for undiagnosed exudates; this fluid is a diuresed transudate.
why_not.C: ADA helps diagnose tuberculous pleurisy in lymphocytic exudates with a compatible risk profile — not this case.
why_not.D: Serial cytology chases malignancy in an exudate that isn't really an exudate.
why_not.E: Indwelling catheters manage recurrent malignant or refractory effusions after medical therapy has been optimized.

questions.pearl: Diuretics make transudates look exudative. Albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL or pleural NT-proBNP >1,500 rescues the diagnosis.
references: Light RW. Pleural Diseases, 6th ed.
Porcel JM. Pleural fluid NT-proBNP in heart failure, Am J Med 2004
BTS Pleural Disease Guideline 2023
questions.image_query: Light's criteria pleural effusion transudate exudate table

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with COPD (post-bronchodilator FEV₁ 45% predicted) quit smoking 2 years ago after 35 pack-years. CT shows centrilobular emphysema, upper-lobe predominant. Because of a family history of “emphysema,” α₁-antitrypsin testing was done: serum level 88 mg/dL (reference 100–200 mg/dL by nephelometry); phenotype PiMZ. Liver enzymes and elastography are normal.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management regarding his α₁-antitrypsin result?

options.A: Begin weekly IV α₁-antitrypsin augmentation therapy
options.C: Repeat phenotyping with genotyping before any COPD therapy
options.D: Begin augmentation only if his FEV₁ falls below 30%
options.E: No augmentation; standard COPD management and offering testing to first-degree relatives

questions.explanation: PiMZ heterozygotes have mildly reduced AAT levels (as here) that are well above the protective threshold (~11 µM, about 57 mg/dL by nephelometry). Their emphysema is driven mainly by smoking. Augmentation therapy is indicated for severe deficiency (e.g., PiZZ, null alleles) with levels below the threshold and airflow obstruction — not for MZ. He needs standard COPD care, continued abstinence, and testing offered to relatives.

why_not.A: Augmentation has evidence (slowed CT density loss) only in severe deficiency; it isn't recommended for MZ.
why_not.B: His liver tests and stiffness are normal; MZ is a modest cofactor for liver disease, not an indication for transplant.
why_not.C: The phenotype and level are concordant; further testing won't change management.
why_not.D: MZ isn't an indication for augmentation at any FEV₁; with severe deficiency, augmentation is typically considered at FEV₁ 30–65%, not delayed until <30%.

questions.pearl: Augmentation = severe deficiency (ZZ, null) with level <11 µM (~57 mg/dL). MZ: quit smoking, standard COPD care, test the family.
references: ATS/ERS Statement on AATD
Sandhaus RA et al. Alpha-1 Foundation Clinical Practice Guidelines, Chronic Obstr Pulm Dis 2016
questions.image_query: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency panlobular emphysema lower lobe CT

questions.stem:
A 32-year-old woman has progressive exertional dyspnea and one exertional presyncopal episode. Evaluation excludes left heart disease, lung disease, chronic thromboembolic disease (normal V/Q scan), connective tissue disease, HIV, portal hypertension, and drug or toxin exposure. Right heart catheterization results are shown.
BaselineInhaled NO 20 ppm
Mean PAP54 mmHg36 mmHg
PAWP8 mmHg8 mmHg
Cardiac output4.0 L/min4.4 L/min
PVR11.5 WU6.4 WU
Right atrial pressure9 mmHg8 mmHg
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?

options.A: Initial dual oral therapy with ambrisentan and tadalafil
options.E: High-dose calcium-channel blocker (e.g., nifedipine) with close reassessment

questions.explanation: This is idiopathic PAH with a positive acute vasoreactivity test: mean PAP falls by ≥10 mmHg to an absolute value ≤40 mmHg with unchanged or increased cardiac output (here 54→36 mmHg, CO 4.0→4.4). Roughly 10% of IPAH patients meet this definition, and they can do very well on high-dose calcium-channel blockers (nifedipine, diltiazem, or amlodipine — not verapamil). Response must be reassessed at 3–6 months (including repeat catheterization); non-sustained responders move to PAH-specific therapy.

why_not.A: Upfront combination therapy is standard for low- or intermediate-risk patients who are not vasoreactive.
why_not.B: Parenteral prostacyclin is for high-risk patients (e.g., WHO FC IV, syncope with RV failure, very high NT-proBNP) or non-responders.
why_not.C: Riociguat is used for CTEPH and as an alternative to a PDE-5 inhibitor, not first-line in vasoreactive IPAH.
why_not.D: Transplant referral is for patients who stay at intermediate-high or high risk despite maximal medical therapy.

questions.pearl: IPAH/heritable/drug-induced PAH: always test vasoreactivity. ΔmPAP ≥10 to ≤40 with CO maintained = CCB candidate (≈10%).
references: 2022 ESC/ERS Guidelines for Pulmonary Hypertension
7th World Symposium on Pulmonary Hypertension 2024
questions.image_query: right heart catheterization vasoreactivity testing nitric oxide pulmonary arterial hypertension

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman has 3 months of 6–8 watery, non-bloody stools a day, including at night. She started sertraline and lansoprazole 6 months ago. Celiac serology and stool studies, including C. difficile, are negative. Colonoscopy is macroscopically normal; random biopsies show a thickened subepithelial collagen band and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.
questions.question: In addition to reviewing her medications, which of the following is the most effective treatment?
questions.explanation: This is collagenous colitis, a form of microscopic colitis associated with PPIs, SSRIs, and NSAIDs. Oral budesonide is the most effective induction (and, if needed, maintenance) therapy, with high remission rates and little systemic steroid exposure.

why_not.B: Mesalamine wasn't superior to placebo in randomized trials.
why_not.C: Systemic prednisone is less effective and more toxic than budesonide.
why_not.D: Loperamide relieves symptoms in mild disease but doesn't induce histologic remission.
why_not.E: Anti-TNF therapy is reserved for budesonide-refractory disease.

questions.pearl: Chronic watery diarrhea, normal colonoscopy → random biopsies. Microscopic colitis → budesonide; stop PPIs, SSRIs, and NSAIDs if possible.
references: AGA 2016 Clinical Practice Guideline on Microscopic Colitis
European Microscopic Colitis Group 2021 guideline
questions.image_query: collagenous colitis histology thickened subepithelial collagen band

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman completed 10 days of oral vancomycin for a first episode of C. difficile infection 3 weeks ago. She now again has 7 unformed stools a day; toxin testing is positive. WBC is 11,000/µL and creatinine is at baseline. She has no ileus or hypotension. She takes omeprazole without a clear indication.
questions.question: In addition to discontinuing omeprazole, which of the following is the preferred treatment?

options.B: Repeat a standard 10-day course of oral vancomycin
options.C: Fecal microbiota transplantation now, without antibiotics

questions.explanation: For a first recurrence, the 2021 IDSA/SHEA update prefers fidaxomicin (standard or extended-pulsed), which has lower subsequent recurrence rates than vancomycin. A tapered-pulsed vancomycin regimen is an acceptable alternative. Microbiome therapies (FMT or approved live biotherapeutics) are recommended after ≥2 recurrences, given after a course of antibiotics.

why_not.A: Metronidazole is inferior and no longer recommended for recurrence.
why_not.B: Repeating the same standard course has a high re-recurrence rate; if vancomycin is used, give a taper-pulse.
why_not.C: Microbiota therapy is for the second or later recurrence, after antibiotic treatment.
why_not.D: IV vancomycin doesn't reach the colonic lumen.

questions.pearl: CDI: initial → fidaxomicin (or vancomycin); 1st recurrence → fidaxomicin (or vancomycin taper-pulse); ≥2 recurrences → microbiota therapy after antibiotics.
references: Johnson S et al. IDSA/SHEA 2021 Focused Update on CDI, Clin Infect Dis 2021
Kelly CR et al. ACG 2021 CDI Guideline
questions.image_query: pseudomembranous colitis colonoscopy

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has iron-deficiency anemia unresponsive to oral iron, bloating, and loose stools. She eats a regular gluten-containing diet. She has had recurrent sinusitis since childhood. Tissue transglutaminase IgA is <1 U/mL (negative). Total serum IgA is <5 mg/dL.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Deamidated gliadin peptide IgG and/or tTG IgG
options.D: Empiric gluten-free diet and reassess in 3 months

questions.explanation: She has selective IgA deficiency (also suggested by recurrent sinusitis), which is ~10–15 times more common in celiac disease and makes IgA-based tests falsely negative. The next step is IgG-based serology (DGP-IgG and/or tTG-IgG) while she is still eating gluten, followed by duodenal biopsy if positive or if suspicion remains high.

why_not.B: The negative tTG-IgA is uninterpretable without measurable IgA.
why_not.C: HLA typing has a high negative predictive value but low specificity; it's used when serology/histology are unreliable (e.g., already gluten-free), not as the next step here.
why_not.D: Going gluten-free before testing renders serology and histology unreliable.
why_not.E: Capsule endoscopy is for complicated or nonresponsive disease, not initial diagnosis.

questions.pearl: Always check total IgA with tTG-IgA. IgA deficient → DGP-IgG/tTG-IgG.
references: Rubio-Tapia A et al. ACG Clinical Guideline: Celiac Disease, Am J Gastroenterol 2023

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man has dyspepsia; urea breath test is positive for H. pylori. He has never been treated. He had anaphylaxis to amoxicillin as a teenager (confirmed in records). He takes no other medications. Antibiotic susceptibility testing is not available.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: PPI, clarithromycin, and amoxicillin for 14 days
options.C: Omeprazole, amoxicillin, and rifabutin for 14 days
options.D: PPI, bismuth, tetracycline, and metronidazole for 14 days
options.E: PPI, levofloxacin, and amoxicillin for 14 days

questions.explanation: With unknown susceptibility, the ACG 2024 guideline prefers optimized bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days in treatment-naive patients. It is the only listed regimen without amoxicillin, so it's also the right choice for his true penicillin anaphylaxis. Confirm eradication ≥4 weeks after therapy (and ≥2 weeks off PPI).

why_not.A: Contains amoxicillin, and empiric clarithromycin triple therapy is discouraged unless susceptibility is known, because of widespread resistance.
why_not.B: Vonoprazan dual therapy depends on amoxicillin.
why_not.C: Rifabutin triple therapy also contains amoxicillin.
why_not.E: Contains amoxicillin, and levofloxacin regimens are reserved for known susceptibility because of high quinolone resistance.

questions.pearl: H. pylori: unknown susceptibility → bismuth quadruple × 14 days. It's also the go-to for penicillin allergy. Test for cure.
references: Chey WD et al. ACG Clinical Guideline: Treatment of H. pylori Infection, Am J Gastroenterol 2024

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back for 10 hours. Lipase is 2,300 U/L. Ultrasound shows gallstones without biliary dilation; bilirubin and ALT are normal. BP 128/74 mmHg, HR 102/min, BUN 22 mg/dL, hematocrit 41%. She has no organ failure. She is hungry and asks when she can eat.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Lactated Ringer's 20 mL/kg bolus followed by 3 mL/kg/h
options.B: Moderate, goal-directed lactated Ringer's and an oral diet as tolerated within 24 hours
options.C: NPO, nasogastric tube, and parenteral nutrition

questions.explanation: In the WATERFALL trial, aggressive fluid resuscitation (20 mL/kg bolus then 3 mL/kg/h) caused more fluid overload without improving outcomes and was stopped early. Current guidance favors moderate, goal-directed lactated Ringer's (e.g., 1.5 mL/kg/h, with a 10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolemic), reassessed frequently. Early oral feeding as tolerated is safe and reduces complications compared with keeping patients NPO. Cholecystectomy should be done during this admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis.

why_not.A: This is the WATERFALL aggressive arm: more volume overload, no benefit.
why_not.C: Routine NPO, NG decompression, and TPN are outdated; enteral (oral) feeding is preferred and TPN raises infection risk.
why_not.D: Prophylactic antibiotics don't prevent infected necrosis and aren't recommended.
why_not.E: Urgent ERCP is for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction, neither of which is present.

questions.pearl: Pancreatitis: moderate LR (not aggressive), feed early, no prophylactic antibiotics, same-admission cholecystectomy for gallstone disease.
references: de-Madaria E et al. WATERFALL, NEJM 2022
Tenner S et al. ACG Guideline: Management of Acute Pancreatitis, Am J Gastroenterol 2024

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with cirrhosis and ascites has abdominal discomfort and mild confusion. Temperature 37.9°C, BP 104/60 mmHg. Paracentesis: ascitic neutrophils 480/µL, total protein 0.9 g/dL; Gram stain negative. Serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL (baseline 0.8), BUN 34 mg/dL, bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL. IV cefotaxime is started.
questions.question: Which additional intervention most improves her survival?

options.B: Furosemide and spironolactone at higher doses
options.D: IV albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3

questions.explanation: Ascitic neutrophils ≥250/µL establish SBP. In patients with SBP and creatinine >1 mg/dL, BUN >30 mg/dL, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL, adding IV albumin (1.5 g/kg at diagnosis, 1 g/kg on day 3) to antibiotics reduced renal failure and mortality (Sort et al.).

why_not.A: Large-volume paracentesis during active SBP and AKI risks worsening circulatory dysfunction.
why_not.B: Diuretics should be held in SBP with AKI.
why_not.C: Midodrine/octreotide is an alternative vasoconstrictor regimen for HRS-AKI, not a substitute for albumin in SBP.
why_not.E: Broader coverage is reserved for nosocomial SBP, recent β-lactam exposure, or known resistant organisms.

questions.pearl: SBP + (Cr >1, BUN >30, or bili >4) → albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3.
references: Sort P et al. NEJM 1999
Biggins SW et al. AASLD Guidance on Ascites, SBP, HRS, Hepatology 2021

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with heavy daily alcohol use developed jaundice 3 weeks after his last drink. On admission: bilirubin 18.2 mg/dL, INR 2.1, Maddrey discriminant function 61, MELD 29. Infection, GI bleeding, and HRS were excluded, and he started prednisolone 40 mg daily. On day 7 his bilirubin is 20.4 mg/dL; Lille score is 0.62. He is alert and has no new infection.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Continue prednisolone to complete 28 days, then taper

questions.explanation: A Lille score >0.45 at day 7 defines nonresponse to corticosteroids. Nonresponders get no survival benefit from continuing steroids and carry a markedly higher risk of infection, so prednisolone should be stopped. Management then focuses on supportive care, nutrition, alcohol-use-disorder treatment and, at selected centers, evaluation for early liver transplantation.

why_not.A: Continuing steroids in nonresponders increases infection risk without benefit.
why_not.B: Pentoxifylline adds no benefit to prednisolone (STOPAH) and doesn't rescue nonresponders.
why_not.C: There is no evidence for higher doses; toxicity would rise.
why_not.E: NAC has been studied only in combination with prednisolone, started at day 1; it isn't salvage monotherapy.

questions.pearl: Severe AH: steroids if MDF ≥32 or MELD >20; check Lille at day 4–7 — >0.45 means stop.
references: Crabb DW et al. AASLD Practice Guidance on Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease, Hepatology 2020
Louvet A et al. Hepatology 2007 (Lille model)
ACG 2024 Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease Guideline

questions.stem:
A 66-year-old man with newly diagnosed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is about to begin R-CHOP. Pretreatment hepatitis B testing is shown. ALT is normal.
TestResultReference
HBsAgNegative
Anti-HBc (total)Positive
Anti-HBs48 mIU/mL
HBV DNANot detected
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: No action; he has natural immunity
options.B: Start entecavir before chemotherapy and continue for at least 12 months after the last rituximab dose
options.C: Check HBV DNA and ALT every 3 months, treating only if they rise
options.E: Start lamivudine for the duration of chemotherapy only

questions.explanation: This is resolved HBV infection (HBsAg−, anti-HBc+). Covalently closed circular DNA persists in hepatocytes, and anti-CD20 therapy (rituximab) carries a high reactivation risk even in HBsAg-negative patients, with potentially fulminant hepatitis. Guidelines recommend prophylaxis with a high-barrier antiviral (entecavir or tenofovir), started before or with chemotherapy and continued ≥12 months (many experts use 18 months) after the last anti-CD20 dose.

why_not.A: Anti-HBs doesn't protect against reactivation under profound B-cell depletion.
why_not.C: Monitoring with on-demand therapy is an option for lower-risk regimens; anti-CD20 therapy is high risk, and prophylaxis is preferred.
why_not.D: Vaccination plays no role in someone already infected.
why_not.E: Lamivudine has a low resistance barrier, and stopping at the end of chemotherapy invites late reactivation.

questions.pearl: Rituximab + anti-HBc positive (even HBsAg negative) → entecavir/tenofovir prophylaxis, through at least 12–18 months after the last dose.
references: Terrault NA et al. AASLD 2018 Hepatitis B Guidance
AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on HBV reactivation

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has fatigue and arthralgias of the second and third MCP joints. He drinks 1–2 beers a week. Exam shows no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Results: transferrin saturation 82%, ferritin 1,460 ng/mL, ALT 74 U/L, AST 58 U/L, platelets 168,000/µL. HFE testing: C282Y homozygous.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Begin therapeutic phlebotomy; no further liver evaluation is needed
options.C: Assess for advanced fibrosis (elastography and/or liver biopsy) and begin phlebotomy
options.D: Restrict dietary iron and recheck ferritin in 6 months

questions.explanation: In C282Y homozygotes, a ferritin >1,000 ng/mL with elevated aminotransferases (and/or a platelet count <200,000) identifies those at high risk of cirrhosis. Staging fibrosis (biopsy, or noninvasive elastography/MRE) matters because cirrhosis means lifelong HCC surveillance and varices screening even after iron depletion. Therapeutic phlebotomy (target ferritin 50–100 ng/mL) should begin regardless.

why_not.A: Phlebotomy is needed, but skipping fibrosis staging misses the cirrhosis that would require HCC surveillance.
why_not.B: Chelation is for patients who can't undergo phlebotomy (e.g., anemia, poor venous access); phlebotomy is safer and cheaper.
why_not.D: Diet alone doesn't meaningfully reduce iron overload.
why_not.E: Hypogonadism can occur, but pituitary imaging isn't the priority.

questions.pearl: HFE C282Y/C282Y with ferritin >1,000 + high ALT (or platelets <200k) → stage fibrosis. Cirrhosis → HCC surveillance for life.
references: Kowdley KV et al. ACG Clinical Guideline: Hereditary Hemochromatosis, Am J Gastroenterol 2019
EASL 2022 Haemochromatosis Guidelines

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis (MELD 27) is admitted with tense ascites. Over 4 days his creatinine rises from 1.1 to 2.6 mg/dL. Diuretics and lactulose were held, he received IV albumin 1 g/kg/day for 2 days, and his creatinine is unchanged. He takes no nephrotoxins and has no shock or infection (diagnostic paracentesis negative). Urinalysis is bland with <100 mg/dL protein and no hematuria; urine sodium is 6 mEq/L. Renal ultrasound is normal. SpO₂ 97% on room air; no pulmonary edema.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Continue albumin alone for 3 more days

questions.explanation: He meets criteria for HRS-AKI: cirrhosis with ascites, a creatinine rise meeting AKI criteria, no response after 2 days of diuretic withdrawal and albumin, no shock, no nephrotoxins, and no structural kidney disease. Terlipressin plus albumin is the most effective vasoconstrictor regimen outside the ICU (CONFIRM: higher HRS reversal). Check oxygenation and volume status first: terlipressin carries a boxed warning for respiratory failure and should be avoided with SpO₂ <90% or volume overload. Liver transplant evaluation is the definitive therapy.

why_not.A: He has already failed the albumin challenge; vasoconstrictors are needed.
why_not.B: Midodrine/octreotide is substantially less effective than terlipressin and is used only when terlipressin and norepinephrine aren't available.
why_not.C: Renal replacement is for refractory complications or a bridge to transplant, not first-line HRS therapy.
why_not.D: TIPS isn't established first-line therapy for HRS-AKI and is risky at MELD 27.

questions.pearl: HRS-AKI → terlipressin + albumin (check SpO₂ and volume status first); norepinephrine + albumin if in the ICU.
references: Wong F et al. CONFIRM, NEJM 2021
Biggins SW et al. AASLD Guidance 2021
International Club of Ascites HRS-AKI criteria 2015/2024

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has 2 years of dysphagia to solids and liquids with intermittent severe retrosternal chest pain. Endoscopy shows no mass or eosinophilic esophagitis; biopsies are normal. Barium swallow shows a corkscrew appearance with a tapered distal esophagus. High-resolution manometry (10 wet swallows): integrated relaxation pressure 28 mmHg (normal <15), no normal peristalsis, premature contractions (distal latency <4.5 s) in 6 of 10 swallows, and no panesophageal pressurization. CT shows no mediastinal or gastroesophageal-junction lesion.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.B: Laparoscopic Heller myotomy with Dor fundoplication

questions.explanation: Impaired LES relaxation (elevated IRP) with absent peristalsis and premature (spastic) contractions in ≥20% of swallows is type III (spastic) achalasia by Chicago Classification v4.0. Type III has the poorest response to dilation and standard Heller myotomy because the spastic segment extends up the esophageal body. POEM allows a long, tailored myotomy covering the spastic segment and has the best outcomes for type III.

why_not.A: Pneumatic dilation works best for type II and poorly for type III.
why_not.B: Laparoscopic myotomy is usually limited to the distal esophagus and may not cover the spastic segment.
why_not.D: Botulinum toxin is temporary and reserved for poor procedural candidates.
why_not.E: Calcium-channel blockers are minimally effective and only for patients who can't undergo definitive therapy.

questions.pearl: Achalasia subtypes: I (no pressurization) and II (panesophageal pressurization) → POEM, Heller, or dilation; II responds best. III (spastic) → POEM.
references: Vaezi MF et al. ACG Clinical Guideline: Achalasia, Am J Gastroenterol 2020
Yadlapati R et al. Chicago Classification v4.0, Neurogastroenterol Motil 2021
questions.image_query: type III achalasia high resolution manometry spastic

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis presents with hematemesis. He is resuscitated with a restrictive transfusion strategy and given IV octreotide and ceftriaxone. Endoscopy at 8 hours shows actively spurting esophageal varices, successfully banded. Child-Pugh score is C11 (bilirubin 3.4 mg/dL, albumin 2.6 g/dL, INR 1.9, moderate ascites, no encephalopathy); MELD 21. Echocardiogram is normal, and he has no hepatocellular carcinoma or portal vein thrombosis.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Continue octreotide for 5 days, then start a nonselective β-blocker with repeat banding
options.D: Start carvedilol today and discharge when stable
options.E: Urgent liver transplant listing in place of further portal-pressure therapy

questions.explanation: Patients at high risk of treatment failure after variceal hemorrhage — Child-Pugh C 10–13, or Child B >7 with active bleeding at endoscopy, or HVPG >20 mmHg — have better survival with pre-emptive (early) covered TIPS within 72 hours (ideally within 24) than with standard drugs plus banding. Child C 14–15 is generally excluded because of futility.

why_not.A: Standard therapy is appropriate for Child A and lower-risk Child B patients, but in Child C it leads to more rebleeding and death.
why_not.B: Balloon tamponade is a temporizing bridge for uncontrolled bleeding; his bleeding is controlled.
why_not.D: Starting a β-blocker early is part of standard care, but it isn't enough for him and discharge without early TIPS ignores the high rebleeding risk.
why_not.E: Transplant evaluation is appropriate, but it doesn't replace early TIPS during the acute bleeding window.

questions.pearl: Variceal bleed with Child C 10–13 (or B >7 actively bleeding): pre-emptive TIPS within 72 h.
references: de Franchis R et al. Baveno VII Consensus, J Hepatol 2022
García-Pagán JC et al. NEJM 2010
Kaplan DE et al. AASLD 2023 Portal Hypertension Guidance
questions.image_query: TIPS transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt diagram

questions.stem:
A 19-year-old woman has 1 week of jaundice and is now confused (grade 2 encephalopathy). She takes no medications or supplements; acetaminophen level is undetectable. Viral hepatitis serologies and autoimmune markers are negative. Laboratory results are shown.
TestResultReference
AST / ALT284 / 92 U/L<40
Alkaline phosphatase28 U/L40–130
Total bilirubin16.8 mg/dL<1.2
INR3.20.9–1.1
Hemoglobin8.1 g/dL12–16
Reticulocytes9%0.5–2.5
Haptoglobin<10 mg/dL30–200
Direct antiglobulin testNegative
Uric acid1.4 mg/dL2.5–6.5
Ceruloplasmin14 mg/dL20–35
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.E: Urgent transfer to a liver transplant center for listing

questions.explanation: Acute liver failure (coagulopathy plus encephalopathy) in a young patient with Coombs-negative hemolysis, a disproportionately low alkaline phosphatase (ALP:bilirubin ratio <4), and AST:ALT >2.2 is the signature of fulminant Wilson disease; low uric acid reflects renal tubular dysfunction. Copper is released from necrotic hepatocytes, causing hemolysis. Fulminant Wilson disease is almost universally fatal without liver transplantation, which cures the metabolic defect. Plasma exchange or albumin dialysis can lower copper as a bridge, but transfer and listing must not be delayed.

why_not.A: Chelators act too slowly for fulminant failure, and penicillamine can cause paradoxical worsening.
why_not.B: Trientine and zinc are maintenance or chronic therapy, not rescue for ALF with encephalopathy.
why_not.C: Steroids help autoimmune hepatitis, which is excluded here and doesn't cause DAT-negative hemolysis with a low ALP.
why_not.D: NAC is given in acetaminophen ALF and may help early non-acetaminophen ALF, but it doesn't substitute for transplantation in fulminant Wilson disease.

questions.pearl: ALF + DAT-negative hemolysis + low ALP (ALP/bili <4) + AST/ALT >2.2 = fulminant Wilson → transplant center now.
references: Korman JD et al. Hepatology 2008 (ALP:bilirubin and AST:ALT ratios)
Schilsky ML et al. AASLD 2022 Wilson Disease Practice Guidance
