questions.stem: A 24-year-old man who smokes has 1 week of hemoptysis and decreased urine output. SpO₂ 90% on room air with bilateral alveolar opacities. Creatinine 4.8 mg/dL (normal 3 months ago); urinalysis shows dysmorphic RBCs and red-cell casts. Anti-GBM antibody titer is markedly elevated; MPO- and PR3-ANCA are negative. Kidney biopsy shows crescents in 60% of glomeruli with linear IgG staining along the glomerular basement membrane.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.D: Supportive hemodialysis and lung-protective ventilation only

questions.explanation: Pulmonary hemorrhage with rapidly progressive GN, circulating anti-GBM antibodies, and linear IgG deposition is anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease. Standard therapy removes the pathogenic antibody and stops its production: daily plasma exchange until antibodies clear, plus cyclophosphamide and high-dose glucocorticoids. Pulmonary hemorrhage is an indication for treatment regardless of renal prognosis. (Smoking increases the risk of lung hemorrhage.)

why_not.A: Rituximab is a second-line option when cyclophosphamide can't be used; alone it acts too slowly.
why_not.B: Steroids alone don't remove circulating antibody or adequately suppress its production.
why_not.D: Withholding immunosuppression in the setting of alveolar hemorrhage is life-threatening.
why_not.E: IVIG has no established role.

questions.pearl: Linear IgG = anti-GBM → PLEX + cyclophosphamide + steroids. Check ANCA too: ~30% are double positive and can relapse like vasculitis.
references: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for Glomerular Diseases (anti-GBM chapter)
questions.image_query: anti-GBM disease linear IgG immunofluorescence

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with hypertension and peripheral artery disease underwent coronary angiography with PCI via the femoral artery 3 weeks ago. Since then his creatinine has risen stepwise from 1.2 to 2.7 mg/dL. He has a lacy, violaceous rash on both feet and painful cyanotic fourth and fifth toes with intact pedal pulses. Eosinophils 920/µL; C3 is low. Urinalysis: trace protein, 2–5 WBC/hpf, no casts.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis from clopidogrel

questions.explanation: A subacute, stepwise creatinine rise weeks after an arterial catheterization, together with livedo reticularis, blue toes with palpable pulses, eosinophilia, and hypocomplementemia, is classic cholesterol crystal embolization. Biopsy (kidney or skin) shows biconvex cholesterol clefts in arterioles. Management is supportive: statin, BP control, and avoiding further vascular procedures; anticoagulation is generally avoided.

why_not.A: Contrast-associated AKI starts within 24–72 hours and peaks at 3–5 days, without skin findings or eosinophilia.
why_not.B: AIN can cause eosinophilia but usually brings pyuria and WBC casts or rash and fever, not livedo and blue toes; clopidogrel is a rare cause.
why_not.C: ATN follows a discrete ischemic insult and produces muddy brown casts.
why_not.E: PAN can cause livedo and kidney injury, but the timing after catheterization, eosinophilia, and low complement fit cholesterol emboli.

questions.pearl: Weeks after a vascular procedure: livedo + blue toes with pulses + eosinophilia + low C3 + stepwise AKI = cholesterol emboli.
references: Scolari F, Ravani P. Atheroembolic renal disease, Lancet 2010
questions.image_query: cholesterol embolization blue toe livedo reticularis

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman collapses after finishing a marathon in 5 hours. She drank water at every station and weighs 2 kg more than before the race. In the medical tent she has a generalized tonic–clonic seizure. Point-of-care sodium is 118 mEq/L. Glucose is normal.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.A: 100 mL of 3% saline IV over 10 minutes, repeated up to twice if symptoms persist
options.E: 3% saline infusion at 0.5 mL/kg/h for 24 hours

questions.explanation: Exercise-associated hyponatremia from excessive fluid intake plus non-osmotic ADH release, now with seizures (severe symptoms from cerebral edema). The priority is a quick 4–6 mEq/L rise in sodium to reverse herniation risk: 100 mL (or 150 mL) boluses of 3% saline over ~10 minutes, repeated as needed. These patients have acute hyponatremia, so osmotic demyelination risk is low, but standard rate limits still apply after symptoms resolve.

why_not.B: Isotonic saline barely raises sodium in someone with high ADH and can even lower it.
why_not.C: Restriction is too slow for seizing cerebral edema.
why_not.D: Vaptans are not for emergencies and their effect is unpredictable.
why_not.E: A slow infusion delays the urgent rise needed for severe symptoms.

questions.pearl: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizure, coma): 3% saline 100–150 mL bolus × up to 3, aiming for +4–6 mEq/L.
references: Hew-Butler T et al. Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus Statement, Clin J Sport Med 2015
Spasovski G et al. European Hyponatraemia Guideline 2014
questions.image_query: exercise associated hyponatremia marathon

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with bipolar disorder well controlled on lithium for 15 years reports thirst and urinating about 6 L/day. Serum sodium 146 mEq/L, serum osmolality 301 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 110 mOsm/kg. After desmopressin, urine osmolality rises to 128 mOsm/kg. Lithium level is therapeutic; eGFR is 72. Her psychiatrist strongly prefers that she stay on lithium.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: A minimal response to desmopressin (<50% rise in urine osmolality) confirms nephrogenic DI, here from lithium, which enters principal cells through the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) and downregulates aquaporin-2. Amiloride blocks ENaC, limiting lithium uptake into these cells, and reduces polyuria without raising lithium levels.

why_not.A: The kidney is resistant to ADH; desmopressin doesn't help.
why_not.B: Thiazides reduce polyuria but increase proximal lithium reabsorption and can cause lithium toxicity; if used, it's with close level monitoring.
why_not.C: Restricting water in a patient who can't concentrate urine causes dangerous hypernatremia.
why_not.E: Demeclocycline causes nephrogenic DI; it's used to treat SIADH.

questions.pearl: Lithium NDI → amiloride (blocks lithium entry via ENaC). Thiazides work but raise lithium levels.
references: Christ-Crain M et al. Diabetes insipidus, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2019
Batlle DC et al. NEJM 1985 (amiloride for lithium NDI)
questions.image_query: lithium nephrogenic diabetes insipidus ENaC aquaporin 2 principal cell

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man without diabetes has CKD attributed to hypertensive nephrosclerosis: eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73 m² (stable over 6 months), urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 450 mg/g. He takes losartan 100 mg daily and amlodipine. BP 126/78 mmHg; potassium 4.8 mEq/L. HbA1c 5.4%.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to slow CKD progression?
questions.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce kidney failure, cardiovascular death, and hospitalization in CKD with or without diabetes (DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY). KDIGO recommends them for patients with eGFR ≥20 and UACR ≥200 mg/g (or heart failure), on top of maximally tolerated RAAS blockade. Expect an initial, hemodynamic eGFR dip of a few points; it is not a reason to stop.

why_not.B: ACEi + ARB increased hyperkalemia and AKI without renal benefit (VA NEPHRON-D, ONTARGET).
why_not.C: Finerenone's kidney benefit was shown in type 2 diabetes (FIDELIO/FIGARO); he doesn't have diabetes.
why_not.D: Steroidal MRAs lower albuminuria but raise hyperkalemia risk at this eGFR and lack hard kidney-outcome data.
why_not.E: Bicarbonate is for metabolic acidosis (HCO₃⁻ <18 mEq/L), which isn't described.

questions.pearl: CKD with eGFR ≥20 and UACR ≥200 (diabetic or not) → SGLT2 inhibitor on top of max ACEi/ARB.
references: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for CKD
Heerspink HJL et al. DAPA-CKD, NEJM 2020
EMPA-KIDNEY Collaborative Group, NEJM 2023

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and CKD (eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m²) has persistent hyperkalemia. He takes metformin and amlodipine; he is not on RAAS blockers, NSAIDs, or trimethoprim. Results are shown.
TestResultReference
Na / Cl / HCO₃⁻138 / 112 / 17 mEq/L
Potassium5.9 mEq/L3.5–5.0
Urine pH5.1
Urine Na / K / Cl60 / 18 / 60 mEq/L
Plasma renin activity0.2 ng/mL/h0.6–4.3 (upright)
Plasma aldosterone2 ng/dL4–31
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his acid–base and potassium disorder?
questions.explanation: A normal anion gap acidosis (AG 9) with hyperkalemia, an acidic urine (pH <5.5), a positive urine anion gap (Na + K − Cl = +18, meaning low ammonium excretion), and low renin and aldosterone is type 4 RTA from hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism, very common in diabetic kidney disease. Aldosterone deficiency impairs K⁺ secretion, and the hyperkalemia itself suppresses ammoniagenesis.

why_not.A: Classic distal RTA causes hypokalemia and an inappropriately alkaline urine (pH >5.5).
why_not.B: Proximal RTA causes hypokalemia and bicarbonaturia; often part of Fanconi syndrome.
why_not.D: Diarrhea produces a negative urine anion gap (appropriately high NH₄⁺ excretion) and hypokalemia.
why_not.E: Toluene causes a distal-RTA–like picture with hypokalemia (hippurate also raises the urine anion gap).

questions.pearl: Non-gap acidosis + high K⁺ + urine pH <5.5 + low renin/aldo = type 4 RTA (diabetes). Treat with a low-K diet, loop diuretic or binder; fludrocortisone if no HTN/edema.
references: Palmer BF, Clegg DJ. Physiology and pathophysiology of potassium homeostasis: Core Curriculum 2019, Am J Kidney Dis 2019
Brenner and Rector's The Kidney, 11th ed.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes his acid–base status?

options.A: Anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation only
options.B: Anion gap metabolic acidosis and a concurrent non–anion gap metabolic acidosis
options.C: Anion gap metabolic acidosis and a concurrent respiratory acidosis
options.E: Anion gap metabolic acidosis and a concurrent metabolic alkalosis

questions.explanation: Anion gap = 134 − (82 + 20) = 32 (normal ~12 with normal albumin), so there is an AG metabolic acidosis (ketoacidosis). Delta–delta: the gap rose by ~20, so with a pure AG acidosis HCO₃⁻ should have fallen to about 24 − 20 = 4. It is actually 20, much higher than expected, so a concurrent metabolic alkalosis (from vomiting: HCl loss and volume contraction) is present. Respiratory: Winter's formula predicts PaCO₂ = 1.5(20) + 8 ± 2 = 36–40; measured 37 is appropriate, so there's no separate respiratory disorder. The near-normal pH hides two severe opposing disorders.

why_not.A: Ignores the delta–delta mismatch: HCO₃⁻ is far too high for a gap of 32.
why_not.B: A coexisting non-gap acidosis would make HCO₃⁻ lower than predicted by the gap change, not higher.
why_not.C: PaCO₂ matches Winter's prediction; there's no respiratory acidosis.
why_not.D: HCO₃⁻ and PaCO₂ are both low with an elevated anion gap; the primary process is metabolic.

questions.pearl: Always calculate ΔAG vs ΔHCO₃⁻: HCO₃⁻ higher than predicted = added metabolic alkalosis; lower = added non-gap acidosis.
references: Berend K et al. Physiological approach to assessment of acid–base disturbances, NEJM 2014

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old woman, a professional dancer, has muscle cramps and fatigue. BP 98/62 mmHg. She denies vomiting or use of diuretics or laxatives. Results are shown. Two random urine diuretic screens (including thiazides and loop diuretics) are negative.
TestResultReference
Potassium2.8 mEq/L3.5–5.0
Bicarbonate31 mEq/L22–28
Magnesium1.3 mg/dL1.7–2.2
Plasma renin activity8.2 ng/mL/h0.6–4.3
Urine chloride (spot)74 mEq/L
Urine calcium/creatinine0.03 mg/mg0.1–0.2
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with low-normal BP and high urine chloride points to renal salt wasting (or diuretics), not vomiting. Hypomagnesemia with hypocalciuria is the thiazide-like signature of Gitelman syndrome (loss-of-function SLC12A3 mutations in the NCC cotransporter). With repeatedly negative diuretic screens, surreptitious thiazide use is unlikely.

why_not.A: Vomiting causes avid renal chloride retention (urine Cl⁻ <20 mEq/L), unless the patient vomited within hours of the sample.
why_not.C: Bartter syndrome mimics loop diuretics: normal or high urine calcium, usually normal Mg²⁺, and typically onset in childhood.
why_not.D: Primary aldosteronism causes hypertension with suppressed renin.
why_not.E: Laxative abuse usually causes a non-gap metabolic acidosis (or mild alkalosis with low urine Cl⁻) and low urine Na⁺/Cl⁻.

questions.pearl: Hypokalemic alkalosis, normal/low BP: urine Cl⁻ <20 = vomiting; >20 = diuretic or Bartter/Gitelman. Low Mg + low urine Ca = Gitelman (thiazide-like).
references: Blanchard A et al. Gitelman syndrome: KDIGO Controversies Conference, Kidney Int 2017

questions.stem:
A 44-year-old man is found confused in a homeless shelter. He is somnolent but protecting his airway; BP 112/70 mmHg. No odor is noted by the triage staff. Results are shown. Urine microscopy shows no crystals. Fundoscopy is normal.
TestResultReference
Sodium / chloride / HCO₃⁻140 / 104 / 24 mEq/LAG 8–12
Glucose98 mg/dL70–99
BUN14 mg/dL7–20
Creatinine (Jaffe)1.6 mg/dL0.7–1.2
Measured serum osmolality336 mOsm/kg275–295
Serum ketones (nitroprusside)PositiveNegative
β-Hydroxybutyrate0.2 mmol/L<0.4
Arterial pH7.387.35–7.45
EthanolUndetectable
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.E: Fomepizole plus thiamine, folate, and pyridoxine

questions.explanation: Calculated osmolality = 2(140) + 98/18 + 14/2.8 ≈ 290, so the osmolar gap is ~46, yet the anion gap is normal and there's no acidosis. Positive ketones with a normal β-hydroxybutyrate mean the ketone is acetone. That combination — “ketosis without acidosis” plus an osmolar gap — is isopropyl alcohol, which alcohol dehydrogenase converts to acetone, not to a toxic acid. Acetone also interferes with the Jaffe creatinine assay, producing a falsely high creatinine. Treatment is supportive; dialysis is reserved for refractory hypotension or extremely high levels.

why_not.A: Blocking alcohol dehydrogenase only prolongs CNS depression, because isopropanol itself is the more sedating compound.
why_not.B: Dialysis is reserved for hemodynamic instability or very high levels (roughly >400–500 mg/dL).
why_not.D: Ethanol blocks alcohol dehydrogenase, offers no benefit here, and adds CNS depression.
why_not.E: This cocktail is for ethylene glycol or methanol, which produce a severe anion gap acidosis (and crystals or visual symptoms).

questions.pearl: Osmolar gap + normal AG + acetone = isopropanol → supportive care. Osmolar gap + high-AG acidosis = methanol/ethylene glycol → fomepizole ± dialysis.
references: Kraut JA, Mullins ME. Toxic alcohols, NEJM 2018
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11th ed.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman taking hydrochlorothiazide had 4 days of vomiting and poor intake. She arrived confused with serum sodium 114 mEq/L and potassium 2.9 mEq/L, received 100 mL of 3% saline, then normal saline and potassium. Over the past 6 hours she has passed 1.8 L of dilute urine (urine osmolality 90 mOsm/kg). Ten hours after arrival her sodium is 124 mEq/L and she is more alert.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Continue normal saline at the current rate
options.B: Stop IV fluids and restrict free water
options.D: No change; the sodium is now in a safe range
options.E: IV desmopressin with 5% dextrose in water to relower the sodium

questions.explanation: Her sodium has risen 10 mEq/L in 10 hours, with a brisk aquaresis still under way: volume repletion has switched off ADH, and the thiazide effect has waned. She is at high risk for osmotic demyelination (hypokalemia, malnutrition, initial Na ≤120), for which the limit is ~8 mEq/L in any 24 hours. The next step is to stop the rise and re-lower: desmopressin (to halt water loss) plus D5W to bring sodium back below the 24-hour limit, with sodium checks every 1–2 hours.

why_not.A: More saline in someone already excreting dilute urine accelerates the rise.
why_not.B: Fluid restriction in a patient with an ongoing water diuresis raises sodium further.
why_not.C: Tolvaptan causes free-water loss and would worsen the overcorrection.
why_not.D: The danger is the rate of change, not the absolute value; the trend will continue overnight.

questions.pearl: Brisk dilute urine after volume repletion = impending overcorrection. Proactive or rescue DDAVP + D5W; high-risk limit 8 mEq/L/24 h.
references: Spasovski G et al. European Hyponatraemia Guideline 2014
Verbalis JG et al. Expert panel recommendations, Am J Med 2013
Adrogué HJ et al. Diagnosis and treatment of hyponatremia, Am J Kidney Dis 2022
questions.image_query: central pontine myelinolysis MRI trident

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has had three symptomatic kidney stones in 18 months. She has taken topiramate 100 mg twice daily for migraine prophylaxis for 2 years. Stone analysis: 90% calcium phosphate (apatite). Serum: Na 140, Cl 110, HCO₃⁻ 19 mEq/L, K 3.6 mEq/L, calcium 9.4 mg/dL, PTH normal. 24-hour urine: volume 2.1 L, calcium 230 mg, citrate 110 mg (low), pH 6.9, oxalate and uric acid normal.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Discontinue topiramate in favor of another migraine preventive
options.C: Add potassium citrate and continue topiramate

questions.explanation: Topiramate inhibits carbonic anhydrase, causing a mild hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, marked hypocitraturia, and a persistently alkaline urine. That combination favors calcium phosphate stones (the risk rises with dose and duration). The most effective intervention is to remove the cause by switching to a preventive without carbonic anhydrase inhibition (e.g., a β-blocker, an anti-CGRP agent, or amitriptyline), while maintaining high fluid intake.

why_not.A: Thiazides reduce urinary calcium but don't fix the drug-induced hypocitraturia and alkaline urine driving these stones.
why_not.C: Citrate restores an inhibitor but raises urine pH further, which can promote calcium phosphate precipitation; it isn't preferred while the cause persists.
why_not.D: Allopurinol targets hyperuricosuria and uric acid stones, which aren't present.
why_not.E: Calcium restriction increases oxalate absorption and stone risk and harms bone.

questions.pearl: Calcium phosphate stones + low citrate + urine pH ~7 + mild non-gap acidosis → think topiramate/zonisamide/acetazolamide or distal RTA.
references: Pearle MS et al. AUA Medical Management of Kidney Stones Guideline 2014/2019
Welch BJ et al. Topiramate and kidney stones, Am J Kidney Dis 2006
questions.image_query: calcium phosphate apatite kidney stone

questions.stem:
A 31-year-old woman is admitted 3 weeks after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with headache, BP 172/104 mmHg, and oliguria. She has had no diarrhea. Peripheral smear shows many schistocytes. Results are shown. Daily plasma exchange was started on admission; after 5 sessions, platelets are 88,000/µL, LDH 980 U/L, and she has required two hemodialysis sessions.
TestResultReference
Hemoglobin7.6 g/dL12–16
Platelets58,000/µL150–400k
LDH1,620 U/L<250
Haptoglobin<10 mg/dL30–200
Creatinine4.3 mg/dL0.5–1.0
ADAMTS13 activity64%>60%
Stool Shiga toxin PCRNegative
C362 mg/dL90–180
DATNegative
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: A C5 inhibitor (eculizumab or ravulizumab), with meningococcal vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis

questions.explanation: This is a thrombotic microangiopathy with severe AKI and ADAMTS13 activity well above 10% (not TTP), no Shiga toxin (not STEC-HUS), and a low C3, in the postpartum period — a classic trigger for complement-mediated (atypical) HUS. Plasma exchange gives at most a partial, temporary response. Terminal complement blockade (eculizumab or ravulizumab) is first-line and often restores kidney function. Because C5 blockade sharply raises the risk of meningococcal disease, vaccinate (MenACWY and MenB) and give antibiotic prophylaxis.

why_not.A: Plasma exchange is a bridge while ADAMTS13 results are pending; it doesn't control complement-driven disease and delays effective therapy.
why_not.C: Caplacizumab blocks vWF–platelet interaction in immune TTP (ADAMTS13 <10%).
why_not.D: Rituximab targets anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies in immune TTP (or anti-factor H antibodies, which are uncommon).
why_not.E: Withholding complement inhibition risks permanent ESKD and further TMA.

questions.pearl: TMA + severe AKI + ADAMTS13 >10% + no STEC → complement-mediated HUS → C5 inhibitor (vaccinate against meningococcus).
references: Goodship THJ et al. KDIGO Controversies Conference on aHUS, Kidney Int 2017
Fakhouri F et al. Lancet 2017 (aHUS review)

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old man has 3 months of night sweats, 8-kg weight loss, and polyuria. Spleen tip is palpable. CT shows bulky retroperitoneal and mesenteric lymphadenopathy without lytic bone lesions. He takes no supplements. Results are shown.
TestResultReference
Calcium12.6 mg/dL8.6–10.2
Phosphate4.2 mg/dL2.5–4.5
Intact PTH8 pg/mL15–65
PTHrPUndetectable<2.0 pmol/L
25-OH vitamin D26 ng/mL30–100
1,25-(OH)₂ vitamin D96 pg/mL18–72
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his hypercalcemia?
questions.explanation: PTH-independent hypercalcemia (suppressed PTH) with undetectable PTHrP, normal 25-OH-D, and an elevated 1,25-(OH)₂D indicates unregulated calcitriol production by macrophages expressing 1α-hydroxylase. That occurs in lymphomas (as here, with B symptoms and bulky adenopathy) and granulomatous diseases (sarcoidosis, TB, fungal infections). It responds well to glucocorticoids, which suppress the enzyme, along with treating the lymphoma.

why_not.A: Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy has elevated PTHrP and low or normal 1,25-D.
why_not.B: Osteolytic hypercalcemia (myeloma, breast cancer) doesn't raise 1,25-D, and there are no bone lesions.
why_not.C: Vitamin D intoxication raises 25-OH-D markedly (often >150 ng/mL).
why_not.E: Milk-alkali syndrome brings metabolic alkalosis and AKI from calcium and alkali ingestion, with low 1,25-D.

questions.pearl: Low PTH, low PTHrP, high 1,25-D = granulomas or lymphoma → steroids work.
references: Minisola S et al. The diagnosis and management of hypercalcaemia, BMJ 2015
Walker MD, Shane E. Hypercalcemia: a review, JAMA 2022
questions.image_query: hypercalcemia diagnostic algorithm PTH PTHrP 1,25 vitamin D

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin and empagliflozin had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy 2 days ago and has eaten little since. He now has nausea and malaise. BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 24/min. Glucose 186 mg/dL, Na 138, Cl 104, HCO₃⁻ 10 mEq/L (anion gap 24), venous pH 7.18, β-hydroxybutyrate 5.8 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL.
questions.question: In addition to stopping empagliflozin, which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: IV fluids alone; the ketosis will clear once he eats
options.B: IV insulin infusion with dextrose-containing fluids
options.E: Withhold insulin until glucose exceeds 250 mg/dL

questions.explanation: A severe ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose in a patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor after surgery and fasting is euglycemic DKA. The drug lowers glucose through glycosuria while promoting lipolysis and ketogenesis. Treatment is the same as DKA, with a twist: an insulin infusion is required to stop ketogenesis, and dextrose must be given from the start so enough insulin can be delivered without hypoglycemia, continuing until the anion gap closes.

why_not.A: Fluids don't reverse insulin deficiency; ketoacidosis will persist or worsen.
why_not.C: Subcutaneous basal insulin alone is too slow and unreliable for severe acidosis.
why_not.D: Bicarbonate is reserved for pH <6.9–7.0.
why_not.E: Waiting for hyperglycemia is exactly the trap: glucose may never rise while acidosis progresses.

questions.pearl: SGLT2i + illness/surgery/fasting + nausea → check ketones even if glucose <250. Insulin drip + D5/D10 from the start. Hold SGLT2i 3 days before surgery.
references: Umpierrez GE et al. Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report, Diabetes Care 2024
FDA 2020 label change: hold SGLT2i before surgery
questions.image_query: euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis SGLT2 inhibitor mechanism

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman who smokes has newly diagnosed Graves hyperthyroidism (TRAb strongly positive). She has eye pain, redness, lid edema, proptosis of 24 mm bilaterally, and intermittent diplopia that began 2 months ago (clinical activity score 5/7). Visual acuity and color vision are normal. She asks about the fastest definitive cure for her hyperthyroidism.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to her hyperthyroidism?

options.A: Methimazole (or thyroidectomy), with treatment of the active orbitopathy and smoking cessation
options.C: Radioactive iodine with low-dose prednisone prophylaxis
options.E: β-Blocker alone until the eye disease burns out

questions.explanation: She has active, moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease (CAS ≥3, proptosis, diplopia). Radioactive iodine can worsen orbitopathy (especially in smokers), so it should be avoided when TED is active and moderate-to-severe or sight-threatening. Control hyperthyroidism with methimazole (or total thyroidectomy) while the eye disease is treated (IV methylprednisolone, or teprotumumab and other biologics) and she stops smoking.

why_not.B: Unprotected RAI carries the highest risk of TED progression.
why_not.C: Steroid prophylaxis is used with RAI for mild active TED or risk factors, not for active moderate-to-severe disease.
why_not.D: PTU has hepatotoxicity concerns and is reserved for first-trimester pregnancy or thyroid storm.
why_not.E: Hyperthyroidism must be treated; uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis also worsens TED.

questions.pearl: Active moderate-to-severe TED: no RAI. Methimazole or surgery; treat the eyes; stop smoking.
references: Ross DS et al. 2016 ATA Hyperthyroidism Guidelines
Burch HB et al. ATA/ETA Consensus Statement on TED, Thyroid 2022
questions.image_query: Graves ophthalmopathy proptosis lid retraction

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man has paroxysmal headaches, sweating, and palpitations. BP 168/102 mmHg. Plasma free normetanephrine is 5 times the upper limit of normal. CT shows a 4.5-cm right adrenal mass with unenhanced attenuation of 38 HU and heterogeneous enhancement. Adrenalectomy is planned.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate preoperative management?

options.A: Metoprolol now, then add an α-blocker
options.B: Proceed directly to surgery within 48 hours
options.E: α-Adrenergic blockade (e.g., doxazosin or phenoxybenzamine) for 7–14 days with liberal salt and fluid intake

questions.explanation: A markedly elevated normetanephrine with a lipid-poor, heterogeneous adrenal mass is a pheochromocytoma. Preoperative α-blockade for 7–14 days, together with a high-sodium diet and fluids to expand the contracted plasma volume, prevents intraoperative hypertensive crises and post-resection hypotension. A β-blocker is added only after adequate α-blockade, to control tachycardia.

why_not.A: β-Blockade first leaves α-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can precipitate a hypertensive crisis or pulmonary edema.
why_not.B: Operating without blockade risks severe intraoperative instability.
why_not.C: Labetalol has far more β than α activity and isn't recommended as initial monotherapy.
why_not.D: Biopsy of a suspected pheochromocytoma can precipitate a crisis and is contraindicated.

questions.pearl: Pheo: α first (7–14 days, plus salt and fluids), β only after; never biopsy.
references: Lenders JWM et al. Endocrine Society Guideline: Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2014
questions.image_query: pheochromocytoma adrenal mass CT

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has taken amiodarone for 3 years for recurrent ventricular tachycardia. He now has weight loss, tremor, and atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. There's no goiter or ophthalmopathy. TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 3.6 ng/dL (0.8–1.8), free T3 elevated. TSH-receptor antibodies are negative. Thyroid ultrasound shows a normal-sized gland with absent vascularity on color Doppler; 24-hour radioiodine uptake is <1%. His cardiologist prefers to continue amiodarone.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.D: Stop amiodarone and observe without other therapy

questions.explanation: Type 2 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis is a destructive thyroiditis: a normal gland, absent Doppler flow, very low uptake, and no TRAb. It responds to glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone 30–40 mg/day tapered over ~3 months). Amiodarone can often be continued when it's essential. Type 1 AIT (iodine-induced excess synthesis in an abnormal gland, with increased vascularity) is treated with thionamides, with or without perchlorate; mixed or uncertain forms get both.

why_not.A: Thionamides block synthesis, but type 2 is a release of preformed hormone; they are ineffective alone.
why_not.B: Uptake is <1% (gland iodine-saturated and destroyed), so RAI won't work.
why_not.D: Amiodarone's long half-life means thyrotoxicosis persists for months, and it's poorly tolerated in a cardiac patient.
why_not.E: This is type 1 therapy for iodine-induced hyperthyroidism in a gland with nodules or latent Graves disease.

questions.pearl: AIT type 1 = hyperfunction (vascular gland) → thionamide ± perchlorate. Type 2 = thyroiditis (avascular) → prednisone.
references: Bartalena L et al. 2018 ETA Guidelines for Amiodarone-Associated Thyroid Dysfunction
Ross DS et al. 2016 ATA Hyperthyroidism Guidelines
questions.image_query: amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis type 1 type 2 Doppler

questions.stem:
A 54-year-old man has 6 months of fatigue, decreased libido, and cold intolerance, and recently bumped into door frames on both sides. Visual field testing shows a bitemporal hemianopia. MRI shows a 2.6-cm sellar mass compressing the optic chiasm. Results are shown.
TestResultReference
TSH1.1 mIU/L0.4–4.5
Free T40.5 ng/dL0.8–1.8
Cortisol (8 AM)2.4 µg/dL6–20
Sodium129 mEq/L135–145
Testosterone / LH142 ng/dL / 1.2 IU/L300–1000 / 1.5–9
Prolactin38 ng/mL<15
questions.question: Which of the following should be done first?

options.B: Restrict fluid to 1 L/day for hyponatremia

questions.explanation: A low free T4 with an inappropriately normal TSH means central hypothyroidism, and the low morning cortisol indicates secondary adrenal insufficiency from a pituitary macroadenoma. Hyponatremia here reflects cortisol deficiency (ADH disinhibition). Glucocorticoid must be replaced before thyroid hormone: levothyroxine accelerates cortisol clearance and raises metabolic demand, which can precipitate adrenal crisis. The mildly elevated prolactin is a stalk effect, not a prolactinoma, at this tumor size.

why_not.A: Starting levothyroxine first can provoke adrenal crisis.
why_not.B: The hyponatremia will correct with glucocorticoid replacement; restriction doesn't treat the cause.
why_not.C: Testosterone can be addressed later; it isn't urgent or life-threatening.
why_not.D: There's no polyuria or hypernatremia to suggest DI, which is uncommon with pituitary adenomas before surgery.

questions.pearl: Low FT4 + normal TSH = central hypothyroidism. Check cortisol, and replace steroids before thyroxine.
references: Fleseriu M et al. Endocrine Society Guideline: Hormonal Replacement in Hypopituitarism, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2016
questions.image_query: pituitary macroadenoma MRI optic chiasm compression

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman has received denosumab 60 mg every 6 months for 4 years (8 doses), with lumbar spine T-score improving from −2.9 to −2.2 and no fractures. She wants to stop injections. Her last dose was 5 months ago. eGFR is 70, and calcium and 25-OH vitamin D are normal. She has good dentition.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?

options.A: Stop denosumab and give zoledronic acid at about the time the next denosumab dose would be due
options.B: Stop denosumab and repeat DXA in 2 years
options.C: Lengthen the denosumab interval to once yearly
options.E: Continue calcium and vitamin D only

questions.explanation: Stopping denosumab causes a rebound surge in bone turnover, rapid loss of the BMD gained, and an increased risk of multiple vertebral fractures within months. Denosumab should not be stopped without follow-on antiresorptive therapy, usually zoledronic acid given about 6 months after the last injection (with turnover markers checked and sometimes a repeat dose), or an oral bisphosphonate.

why_not.B: Unprotected discontinuation risks rebound vertebral fractures.
why_not.C: Delayed or less frequent dosing allows the same rebound; denosumab must be given every 6 months.
why_not.D: Raloxifene is too weak to prevent the rebound.
why_not.E: Calcium and vitamin D don't prevent the post-denosumab turnover surge.

questions.pearl: Never stop denosumab cold. Bridge with a bisphosphonate (zoledronate ~6 months after the last dose).
references: Tsourdi E et al. ECTS position statement on denosumab discontinuation, Bone 2017/2021
Eastell R et al. Endocrine Society Osteoporosis Guideline 2019/2020
questions.image_query: denosumab discontinuation rebound vertebral fractures

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old nurse has 2 months of palpitations, heat intolerance, and a 7-kg weight loss. She has no neck pain or recent pregnancy, and no iodinated contrast or amiodarone exposure. The thyroid is not palpable or tender, and there's no ophthalmopathy. Results are shown. Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are negative.
TestResultReference
TSH<0.01 mIU/L0.4–4.5
Free T42.9 ng/dL0.8–1.8
Total T3260 ng/dL80–180
24-h radioiodine uptake1%10–30%
Thyroglobulin<0.5 ng/mL1.5–38
TSH-receptor antibodyNegative
ESR8 mm/h<20
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Thyrotoxicosis with near-zero radioiodine uptake narrows the differential to thyroiditis, iodine load, ectopic thyroid tissue, or exogenous hormone. The discriminator is serum thyroglobulin: high in thyroiditis (gland destruction) and struma ovarii, suppressed when hormone is taken exogenously (TSH suppression shuts the gland down). An undetectable thyroglobulin with negative anti-Tg antibodies (which would invalidate the assay) points to surreptitious thyroid hormone use.

why_not.A: Painless thyroiditis releases stored hormone and thyroglobulin, so Tg is elevated.
why_not.B: Subacute thyroiditis causes a tender gland, high ESR/CRP, and high Tg.
why_not.D: Struma ovarii shows pelvic uptake and an elevated Tg.
why_not.E: Graves disease has high, diffuse uptake and positive TRAb.

questions.pearl: Low-uptake thyrotoxicosis: thyroglobulin high = thyroiditis; thyroglobulin undetectable = exogenous hormone (check anti-Tg Ab).
references: Ross DS et al. 2016 ATA Hyperthyroidism Guidelines
questions.image_query: thyrotoxicosis low radioiodine uptake differential thyroglobulin

questions.stem:
A 41-year-old man has asymptomatic hypercalcemia found on routine labs. His mother had “high calcium” and underwent neck exploration that didn't normalize her calcium. He has no kidney stones or fractures. Results are shown.
TestResultReference
Calcium10.9 mg/dL8.6–10.2
Intact PTH58 pg/mL15–65
25-OH vitamin D34 ng/mL30–100
Magnesium2.4 mg/dL1.7–2.2
24-h urine calcium62 mg100–300
Ca/Cr clearance ratio0.006
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.D: CASR genetic testing, with no parathyroid surgery
options.E: Repeat calcium in 1 year and refer for surgery if it rises

questions.explanation: Mild PTH-dependent hypercalcemia with a calcium/creatinine clearance ratio <0.01 (here 0.006), a vitamin-D–replete patient, and a family history of failed parathyroid surgery is familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia. Inactivating mutations in the calcium-sensing receptor raise the PTH set point and increase renal calcium reabsorption. FHH is benign and doesn't respond to parathyroidectomy. Confirm with CASR (or GNA11/AP2S1) testing, and avoid surgery.

why_not.A: Surgery doesn't correct FHH; his mother's experience illustrates the trap.
why_not.B: Cinacalcet is rarely needed; FHH is usually asymptomatic.
why_not.C: Bone density is generally normal; no therapy is indicated.
why_not.E: Calcium is typically stable for life; the diagnosis should be established now so surgery is avoided.

questions.pearl: Ca/Cr clearance ratio <0.01 with mild hypercalcemia → FHH (CASR). Don't operate.
references: Bilezikian JP et al. Fifth International Workshop on Primary Hyperparathyroidism, J Bone Miner Res 2022
questions.image_query: calcium sensing receptor parathyroid kidney FHH

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with obesity (BMI 41 kg/m²) and type 2 diabetes reports low libido and fatigue. Two fasting morning total testosterone levels are 240 and 255 ng/dL (reference 264–916). SHBG is 12 nmol/L (reference 17–56). LH is 4.1 IU/L (normal). Prolactin is normal. He doesn't use opioids or glucocorticoids.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.E: Measure free testosterone by equilibrium dialysis (or calculate it from reliable total T, SHBG, and albumin)

questions.explanation: Obesity and insulin resistance lower SHBG, which lowers total testosterone even when the biologically active free fraction is normal. When total T is near the lower limit, or SHBG is altered, the Endocrine Society recommends measuring free testosterone by equilibrium dialysis (or a reliable calculation) before diagnosing hypogonadism. If free T is low, the inappropriately normal LH would indicate secondary hypogonadism, which is often functional in obesity and improves with weight loss.

why_not.A: Treating without confirming true androgen deficiency risks unnecessary therapy (erythrocytosis, fertility suppression).
why_not.B: Pituitary imaging is for confirmed secondary hypogonadism with very low testosterone (<150 ng/dL), other pituitary abnormalities, or mass symptoms.
why_not.C: Clomiphene is off-label and premature without a confirmed diagnosis.
why_not.D: Klinefelter syndrome causes primary hypogonadism with high LH.

questions.pearl: Low total T + low SHBG (obesity, diabetes) → measure free T before labeling hypogonadism.
references: Bhasin S et al. Endocrine Society Guideline: Testosterone Therapy in Men with Hypogonadism, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018

questions.stem:
A 42-year-old woman has had episodes of confusion and sweating before breakfast and after missed meals, relieved by eating; she has gained 6 kg. Her mother, who lives with her, takes glipizide. During a supervised fast, she develops neuroglycopenic symptoms at 14 hours. Results at that time are shown. After 1 mg IV glucagon, glucose rises by 38 mg/dL.
TestResultReference
Glucose42 mg/dL
Insulin14 µU/mL
C-peptide2.1 ng/mL
Proinsulin22 pmol/L
β-Hydroxybutyrate0.3 mmol/L
Sulfonylurea/meglitinide screenNegative
Insulin antibodiesNegative
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia (glucose <55 with insulin ≥3 µU/mL, C-peptide ≥0.6 ng/mL, proinsulin ≥5 pmol/L, β-hydroxybutyrate ≤2.7 mmol/L, and a ≥25 mg/dL glucose rise after glucagon) has a short differential: insulinoma, insulin secretagogues, or insulin autoimmune syndrome. A negative secretagogue screen (despite access to glipizide) and negative insulin antibodies leave insulinoma. Next comes localization (CT/MRI, endoscopic ultrasound, or GLP-1 receptor/DOTATATE imaging).

why_not.A: Exogenous insulin suppresses C-peptide and proinsulin.
why_not.C: Sulfonylureas raise insulin and C-peptide, but the drug screen (which covers glipizide) is negative.
why_not.D: Insulin autoimmune syndrome causes very high insulin levels (often >100 µU/mL), typically postprandial, with positive insulin antibodies.
why_not.E: IGF-2–mediated hypoglycemia has suppressed insulin and C-peptide.

questions.pearl: High insulin + high C-peptide + high proinsulin + negative sulfonylurea screen + negative insulin antibodies = insulinoma.
references: Cryer PE et al. Endocrine Society Guideline: Adult Hypoglycemic Disorders, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2009
questions.image_query: insulinoma pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor CT arterial phase

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has hypertension requiring four drugs and spontaneous hypokalemia (K⁺ 3.1 mEq/L). Plasma aldosterone is 28 ng/dL with suppressed renin (PRA <0.2 ng/mL/h). Adrenal CT shows a 1.3-cm left adrenal adenoma and a normal-appearing right adrenal gland. He wants a surgical cure if possible.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.C: Saline infusion suppression test before any other step

questions.explanation: With spontaneous hypokalemia, suppressed renin, and aldosterone >20 ng/dL, primary aldosteronism is established, and the 2025 Endocrine Society guideline allows confirmatory testing to be skipped when the probability is this high. In a surgical candidate the key question is laterality. CT is unreliable after age 35: nonfunctioning incidentalomas are common, and bilateral hyperplasia can coexist, so CT alone sends many patients to the wrong operation. AVS is recommended before adrenalectomy; it can be skipped only in patients <35 with marked PA and a unilateral adenoma.

why_not.A: Operating on CT findings alone risks removing a nonfunctioning nodule while the true source (or bilateral disease) remains.
why_not.B: MRA therapy is right if he doesn't want surgery, but he wants a possible cure, which requires lateralization.
why_not.C: Confirmation can be skipped when hypokalemia, suppressed renin, and high aldosterone coexist.
why_not.E: FDG-PET doesn't lateralize aldosterone production (CXCR4-directed PET is investigational).

questions.pearl: PA + surgical candidate → AVS, unless age <35 with marked PA and a unilateral adenoma.
references: Adler GK et al. Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Aldosteronism, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2025
questions.image_query: adrenal vein sampling primary aldosteronism lateralization

questions.stem:
A 61-year-old woman has a 2.8-cm left adrenal mass found on CT for abdominal pain. The mass is homogeneous with an unenhanced attenuation of 6 HU. She has no plethora, striae, proximal weakness, or easy bruising. She has hypertension on two drugs, prediabetes, and osteopenia. Results are shown.
TestResultReference
Cortisol after 1-mg overnight dexamethasone3.4 µg/dL<1.8
ACTH (morning)7 pg/mL10–60
Plasma free metanephrinesNormal
Aldosterone / reninNormal ratio
DHEA-SLow-normal
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Adrenalectomy, which is indicated for all patients with this result
options.C: Optimize treatment of hypertension, glycemia, and bone health, with an individualized discussion of adrenalectomy
options.D: Repeat adrenal CT at 6 and 12 months

questions.explanation: A homogeneous mass <4 cm with ≤10 HU is a benign lipid-rich adenoma; no further imaging is needed. Cortisol of 1.8–5 µg/dL after 1-mg dexamethasone (here 3.4, with low-normal ACTH) without overt Cushing features is mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS). MACS is associated with hypertension, dysglycemia, osteoporosis, and cardiovascular events. The 2023 ESE/ENSAT guideline recommends screening for and treating these comorbidities, and an individualized decision about adrenalectomy based on age, the degree of cortisol excess, comorbidities, and patient preference.

why_not.A: Surgery isn't automatic for MACS; benefit is uncertain and depends on the individual.
why_not.B: MACS warrants comorbidity assessment and treatment; ignoring it misses modifiable cardiometabolic risk.
why_not.D: A ≤10-HU homogeneous adenoma <4 cm needs no repeat imaging.
why_not.E: Medical cortisol blockade is for overt Cushing syndrome or non-surgical candidates with significant disease, not first-line in MACS.

questions.pearl: Incidentaloma ≤10 HU: no more imaging. Post-1-mg-dex cortisol >1.8 = possible MACS → treat comorbidities, individualize surgery.
references: Fassnacht M et al. ESE/ENSAT Guideline on Adrenal Incidentalomas, Eur J Endocrinol 2023
questions.image_query: adrenal adenoma CT low attenuation lipid rich

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes is admitted in diabetic ketoacidosis. Two days later she has left facial pain and swelling, decreased vision in the left eye, and proptosis. There is a black necrotic eschar on the hard palate. MRI shows left maxillary and ethmoid sinus opacification with orbital extension. Biopsy shows broad, ribbon-like, pauci-septate hyphae branching at right angles.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Liposomal amphotericin B and urgent surgical debridement

questions.explanation: Mucormycosis (Rhizopus or Mucor) thrives in acidosis and hyperglycemia; it invades blood vessels and causes necrotic eschars. Wide, pauci-septate, right-angle–branching hyphae confirm it. Survival depends on high-dose liposomal amphotericin B plus aggressive surgical debridement, and on correcting the ketoacidosis. Isavuconazole or posaconazole are alternatives or step-down options.

why_not.A: Voriconazole has no activity against Mucorales (and breakthrough mucor occurs on it).
why_not.C: Echinocandins are inactive against Mucorales.
why_not.D: Fluconazole has no mold activity.
why_not.E: This is a fungal infection; antibacterials alone are inappropriate.

questions.pearl: DKA + black palatal eschar + broad pauci-septate right-angle hyphae = mucor → liposomal ampho B + surgery. Voriconazole doesn't work.
references: Cornely OA et al. Global guideline for mucormycosis (ECMM/MSG-ERC), Lancet Infect Dis 2019
questions.image_query: mucormycosis palatal eschar

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman on day 12 of induction chemotherapy for AML has a temperature of 38.6°C. ANC is 80/µL. BP 118/70 mmHg, HR 98/min, SpO₂ 98% on room air. Her tunneled central catheter site is clean, the skin and mucosa are intact, chest radiograph is clear, and she has no history of MRSA or resistant gram-negative infection. She is on levofloxacin prophylaxis.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antimicrobial therapy?

options.D: Oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin–clavulanate as an outpatient
options.E: Observe without antibiotics until cultures result

questions.explanation: High-risk febrile neutropenia (AML induction, profound and prolonged neutropenia) requires inpatient IV antipseudomonal β-lactam monotherapy (cefepime, piperacillin–tazobactam, or a carbapenem) started within an hour. Vancomycin is not routinely added; it's for hemodynamic instability, suspected catheter-related or skin/soft-tissue infection, pneumonia, MRSA colonization, or gram-positive cocci in blood cultures.

why_not.A: Empiric vancomycin without a specific indication doesn't improve outcomes and promotes resistance and toxicity.
why_not.B: Empiric antifungals are added for persistent fever after 4–7 days of antibacterials, not at the outset; this regimen is excessive.
why_not.D: Oral outpatient therapy is only for low-risk patients (high MASCC score, short expected neutropenia); she is also on fluoroquinolone prophylaxis.
why_not.E: Delaying antibiotics in neutropenic fever increases mortality.

questions.pearl: Neutropenic fever: antipseudomonal β-lactam within 1 h. Add vancomycin only for specific indications; antifungals if fever persists 4–7 days.
references: Freifeld AG et al. IDSA Febrile Neutropenia Guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2011
Taplitz RA et al. ASCO/IDSA Outpatient Management Guideline 2018
questions.image_query: febrile neutropenia management algorithm

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has 3 weeks of progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough. He has oral thrush. HIV antibody is newly positive; CD4 count is 42 cells/µL. Chest CT shows diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities. LDH 480 U/L. On room air, PaO₂ is 62 mmHg with an A–a gradient of 42 mmHg. Induced sputum is positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii by immunofluorescence. He has no sulfa allergy.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.D: Start ART today, with TMP-SMX once ART is established

questions.explanation: Moderate-to-severe PJP (room-air PaO₂ <70 mmHg or A–a gradient ≥35) benefits from adjunctive glucocorticoids started within 72 hours of anti-Pneumocystis therapy, which reduce respiratory failure and death. TMP-SMX for 21 days is first-line. Start ART within 2 weeks of PJP treatment (early ART reduced AIDS progression and death in ACTG A5164).

why_not.A: Omitting steroids in hypoxemic PJP increases mortality.
why_not.B: Atovaquone is for mild disease or sulfa intolerance; it's less effective.
why_not.C: Pentamidine is a toxic second-line option for severe disease when TMP-SMX can't be used.
why_not.D: PJP treatment can't be delayed; ART follows within 2 weeks.

questions.pearl: PJP with PaO₂ <70 or A–a ≥35 → TMP-SMX + prednisone; ART within 2 weeks.
references: NIH/CDC/IDSA OI Guidelines (Pneumocystis)
Zolopa A et al. ACTG A5164, PLoS One 2009
questions.image_query: Pneumocystis pneumonia CT ground glass

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with diabetes is admitted with fever. Blood cultures grow methicillin-susceptible S. aureus in 4 of 4 bottles. He is treated with IV cefazolin. A transthoracic echocardiogram is negative. On hospital day 5 he still has fevers, and repeat blood cultures from day 3 and day 4 are positive. He now reports new low back pain with point tenderness over L3–L4.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Transesophageal echocardiography and MRI of the lumbar spine
options.D: Plan a total of 14 days of cefazolin

questions.explanation: Persistent bacteremia (>72 hours) on appropriate therapy means an undrained focus or endovascular infection until proven otherwise. A negative TTE doesn't exclude endocarditis, so TEE is needed, and focal spinal tenderness demands MRI for vertebral osteomyelitis or epidural abscess (which may need drainage). Persistent bacteremia also turns this into complicated SAB, requiring at least 4–6 weeks of therapy.

why_not.A: Cefazolin (or an antistaphylococcal penicillin) is superior to vancomycin for MSSA; switching worsens therapy.
why_not.C: Adjunctive rifampin didn't improve outcomes (ARREST) and adds toxicity.
why_not.D: Fourteen days applies only to uncomplicated SAB: cultures clear within 72 h, no endocarditis, no implants, and no metastatic foci.
why_not.E: Gentamicin adds nephrotoxicity without benefit for native-valve S. aureus.

questions.pearl: SAB persistent >72 h → TEE + hunt for metastatic foci (spine, joints, abscess, devices) → complicated course.
references: Liu C et al. IDSA MRSA Guideline 2011
Fowler VG et al. 2023 Duke-ISCVID Endocarditis Criteria
Thwaites GE et al. ARREST, Lancet 2018
questions.image_query: vertebral osteomyelitis epidural abscess MRI

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman returned 10 days ago from visiting family in Ghana; she took no prophylaxis. She has fever, rigors, and is now confused. Temperature 39.6°C, BP 104/62 mmHg. Bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL, creatinine 2.3 mg/dL, glucose 64 mg/dL, platelets 38,000/µL. A thin smear is shown; parasitemia is estimated at 8%.

diagrams.caption: Thin smear, Giemsa (schematic). Note the size of infected cells, number of rings per cell, and the elongated form at lower right.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Delicate ring forms in normal-sized red cells, multiply infected cells, appliqué forms, a banana-shaped gametocyte, high parasitemia, and travel to West Africa indicate Plasmodium falciparum. Impaired consciousness, renal and hepatic dysfunction, and >5% parasitemia define severe malaria. IV artesunate is first-line (it lowered mortality versus quinine in SEAQUAMAT and AQUAMAT) and is available in the US, followed by a full oral ACT course. Watch for delayed post-artesunate hemolysis.

why_not.A: Oral therapy is for uncomplicated malaria in patients who can take it; she has severe disease.
why_not.B: Falciparum from West Africa is chloroquine-resistant.
why_not.D: IV quinidine is no longer available in the US and was inferior to artesunate.
why_not.E: Exchange transfusion is no longer recommended by the CDC as adjunct therapy.

questions.pearl: Severe falciparum (altered mental status, organ dysfunction, parasitemia ≥5%) → IV artesunate, then an oral ACT.
references: CDC Treatment of Malaria: Guidelines for Clinicians (US)
Dondorp AM et al. AQUAMAT, Lancet 2010
questions.image_query: Plasmodium falciparum thin smear ring forms banana gametocyte

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man who grew up in rural Ecuador and moved to the US 16 years ago is diagnosed with immune thrombocytopenia (platelets 9,000/µL with mucosal bleeding). The hematologist plans dexamethasone 40 mg daily for 4 days. CBC also shows an eosinophil count of 900/µL. He has intermittent abdominal discomfort and an occasional itchy, migrating rash on his buttocks.
questions.question: Which of the following should be done in conjunction with starting glucocorticoids?

options.C: Stool ova and parasites ×3; treat only if positive
options.E: No action; eosinophilia is common in ITP

questions.explanation: Strongyloides stercoralis can persist for decades through autoinfection. Eosinophilia, origin from an endemic area, GI symptoms, and a migrating serpiginous rash (larva currens) make chronic infection likely. Glucocorticoids can trigger hyperinfection and dissemination, often fatal with gram-negative sepsis. When steroids can't wait, give empiric ivermectin (and send serology); otherwise test and treat.

why_not.A: Albendazole is less effective than ivermectin for Strongyloides.
why_not.B: Praziquantel treats schistosomes and tapeworms, not Strongyloides.
why_not.C: Stool examination is insensitive (larvae are shed intermittently), and urgent steroids can't wait for repeat testing.
why_not.E: Eosinophilia isn't a feature of ITP; ignoring it risks hyperinfection.

questions.pearl: Before high-dose steroids or immunosuppression in someone from an endemic area, test for (or empirically treat) Strongyloides with ivermectin.
references: Mejia R, Nutman TB. Curr Opin Infect Dis 2012
CDC Strongyloidiasis Resources for Health Professionals
questions.image_query: larva currens strongyloides rash

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis ate raw oysters on the Gulf Coast in July. Within 24 hours he developed fever, hypotension (BP 78/44 mmHg despite fluids), and rapidly enlarging hemorrhagic bullae on both lower legs, with pain out of proportion to the exam findings.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.E: Doxycycline plus ceftazidime, with urgent surgical evaluation

questions.explanation: Septic shock with hemorrhagic bullae after raw oysters in a patient with liver disease (iron overload and impaired immunity) is Vibrio vulnificus infection, with mortality >50%. Treatment is doxycycline plus a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftazidime or ceftriaxone) without delay, plus early surgical debridement or fasciotomy for necrotizing soft-tissue infection.

why_not.A: Broad, but not the recommended regimen and lacking a tetracycline.
why_not.B: Cefazolin doesn't adequately cover Vibrio.
why_not.C: This is the regimen for group A streptococcal necrotizing infection.
why_not.D: TMP-SMX plus an aminoglycoside is an alternative only in specific circumstances; alone it's inadequate.

questions.pearl: Cirrhosis + raw oysters or seawater wound + hemorrhagic bullae + shock = V. vulnificus → doxycycline + ceftazidime + surgery.
references: CDC Vibrio Clinical Guidance
Stevens DL et al. IDSA Skin and Soft Tissue Infection Guideline 2014
questions.image_query: Vibrio vulnificus hemorrhagic bullae leg

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man who sleeps in shelters and outdoors has 3 months of fevers, night sweats, and a 9-kg weight loss. He has excoriations over his trunk, and small whitish eggs are attached to the seams of his clothing. There's a new diastolic murmur. Three sets of blood cultures, drawn before any antibiotics and held for extended incubation, show no growth. TEE shows a 12-mm aortic valve vegetation. Urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria. He has no animal or farm contact and doesn't drink unpasteurized milk.
questions.question: Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Culture-negative endocarditis in a homeless patient with body lice (eggs, or nits, in clothing seams) is classically Bartonella quintana (the agent of trench fever), often affecting the aortic valve and associated with immune-complex glomerulonephritis. Diagnose with high-titer Bartonella IgG (≥1:800) or valve PCR. Treat with doxycycline (6 weeks) plus gentamicin (2 weeks), or rifampin if gentamicin can't be used; many patients need valve surgery.

why_not.A: Q fever endocarditis follows exposure to livestock or parturient animals (phase I IgG ≥1:800).
why_not.B: Whipple endocarditis is rare and typically occurs in middle-aged men with arthralgias, often without fever.
why_not.C: HACEK organisms grow in modern blood culture systems within 5 days.
why_not.E: Brucella follows unpasteurized dairy or livestock exposure.

questions.pearl: Culture-negative IE: homeless + body lice → B. quintana; cats → B. henselae; farm animals → Coxiella.
references: Baddour LM et al. AHA IE Statement 2015
Fournier PE et al. Blood culture–negative endocarditis, Clin Infect Dis 2010
questions.image_query: body lice clothing seams nits Pediculus humanus corporis

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV (CD4 28 cells/µL, not on ART) has 2 weeks of headache and fever. Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 34 cm H₂O, CSF cryptococcal antigen positive, India ink positive. He starts liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine, and daily therapeutic lumbar punctures lower his pressure. He asks when he can start HIV treatment.
questions.question: When should antiretroviral therapy be started?

options.C: After completing 12 months of fluconazole maintenance
options.D: Only once CSF cryptococcal antigen becomes negative
options.E: About 4–6 weeks after starting antifungal therapy

questions.explanation: In cryptococcal meningitis, early ART (within 1–2 weeks) increased mortality (COAT trial), largely from CNS immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome. ART should be deferred ~4–6 weeks after starting antifungal therapy, once induction is complete and consolidation with fluconazole is under way. This is the opposite of most opportunistic infections (e.g., PJP or TB without meningitis), where ART begins within 2 weeks.

why_not.A: Very early ART raised mortality in cryptococcal meningitis.
why_not.B: One week is still in the high-risk window.
why_not.C: Waiting a year leaves him profoundly immunosuppressed and at risk for other opportunistic infections.
why_not.D: CSF antigen can stay positive for months; it isn't a timing criterion.

questions.pearl: Most OIs: start ART within 2 weeks. Cryptococcal (and TB) meningitis: wait ~4–6 weeks. Treat high opening pressure with serial LPs.
references: Boulware DR et al. COAT, NEJM 2014
NIH/CDC/IDSA Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections in Adults with HIV (Cryptococcosis)
questions.image_query: Cryptococcus India ink stain CSF capsule

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man with CKD (eGFR 38) and recent cystoscopy has 3 weeks of fevers and fatigue. All blood cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis, susceptible to ampicillin and vancomycin. TEE shows an 8-mm vegetation on the native mitral valve with moderate regurgitation; there is no abscess or heart failure.
questions.question: Which of the following is the preferred antibiotic regimen?
questions.explanation: Enterococcal endocarditis needs bactericidal synergy. Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (saturating different penicillin-binding proteins) is as effective as ampicillin–gentamicin, with far less nephrotoxicity. It is preferred for patients with CKD or older age, and it also works against high-level aminoglycoside-resistant strains. Duration is 6 weeks.

why_not.B: Effective, but gentamicin in an elderly patient with CKD carries substantial nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity risk.
why_not.C: Vancomycin is reserved for β-lactam allergy or resistance; adding gentamicin compounds nephrotoxicity.
why_not.D: Enterococci are intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins; ceftriaxone works only as a synergy partner.
why_not.E: Daptomycin monotherapy isn't first-line for ampicillin-susceptible E. faecalis endocarditis.

questions.pearl: E. faecalis IE → ampicillin + ceftriaxone × 6 weeks (no aminoglycoside toxicity).
references: Baddour LM et al. AHA Scientific Statement on IE in Adults, Circulation 2015
2023 ESC Guidelines for Endocarditis
questions.image_query: mitral valve vegetation TEE endocarditis

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with HIV on suppressive ART (CD4 450 cells/µL) has 2 weeks of blurred vision and floaters in both eyes. Ophthalmology finds bilateral panuveitis. He has no headache, cranial nerve palsies, or hearing loss. He had a non-pruritic palmar rash a month ago. RPR is reactive at 1:256; TP-PA is reactive.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once
options.B: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly for 3 weeks
options.C: Lumbar puncture, then treat for neurosyphilis only if the CSF VDRL is reactive
options.D: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 million units/day IV for 10–14 days
options.E: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 28 days

questions.explanation: Ocular syphilis (uveitis after a secondary-syphilis rash, with a high-titer RPR) is managed as neurosyphilis, whatever the CSF shows: IV aqueous penicillin G 18–24 MU/day for 10–14 days (or procaine penicillin with probenecid). The CDC notes that a normal CSF exam doesn't rule out ocular syphilis and shouldn't delay treatment. Many experts give a dose of benzathine penicillin weekly for up to 3 weeks afterward. Ocular and otic syphilis are emergencies; delay risks permanent vision loss.

why_not.A: Single-dose benzathine penicillin (primary, secondary, or early latent) doesn't reach adequate CNS or ocular levels.
why_not.B: Three weekly doses treat late latent syphilis, not ocular or neurosyphilis.
why_not.C: CSF can be normal in ocular syphilis; therapy shouldn't hinge on it.
why_not.E: Doxycycline is an alternative for penicillin-allergic early or late latent syphilis, not ocular disease (desensitize instead).

questions.pearl: Ocular or otic syphilis = neurosyphilis regimen (IV penicillin G 10–14 days), even with a normal CSF.
references: Workowski KA et al. CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021
questions.image_query: secondary syphilis palmar rash

questions.stem: A 29-year-old cisgender woman wants HIV prevention. Her male partner has HIV and inconsistent viral suppression; condom use is inconsistent. She was born with a solitary kidney; estimated creatinine clearance is 52 mL/min. HIV antigen/antibody and HIV RNA tests are negative; HBsAg is negative and she is HBV-immune. She has no injection drug use and isn't pregnant.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate PrEP option?
questions.explanation: Each oral option has a disqualifier: TDF/FTC requires CrCl ≥60 mL/min for PrEP; TAF/FTC isn't approved for people exposed through receptive vaginal sex (it wasn't studied in cisgender women); and 2-1-1 dosing is supported only for MSM. Long-acting cabotegravir (approved for cisgender women and superior to TDF/FTC in HPTN 084) needs no renal dose adjustment. Twice-yearly lenacapavir is another newer injectable option.

why_not.B: Not recommended for PrEP with CrCl <60 mL/min.
why_not.C: Not approved for receptive vaginal exposure.
why_not.D: Event-driven dosing has evidence only for anal sex in MSM.
why_not.E: She has substantial ongoing exposure and should be offered effective PrEP.

questions.pearl: PrEP: TDF/FTC needs CrCl ≥60; TAF/FTC not for receptive vaginal sex; 2-1-1 only for MSM; cabotegravir (or lenacapavir) injections work for all.
references: CDC PrEP Clinical Practice Guideline 2021 (update 2024)
Delany-Moretlwe S et al. HPTN 084, Lancet 2022
questions.image_query: HIV PrEP options comparison chart

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is admitted with pyelonephritis and bacteremia. Blood and urine cultures grow Enterobacter cloacae complex. Susceptibility report: ceftriaxone MIC ≤1 (susceptible), cefepime MIC ≤1 (susceptible), piperacillin–tazobactam susceptible, meropenem susceptible. He has been on empiric ceftriaxone for 24 hours and is improving; source control isn't needed. He has no β-lactam allergy.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive therapy?

options.A: Continue ceftriaxone, since the isolate is susceptible

questions.explanation: E. cloacae, Klebsiella aerogenes, and Citrobacter freundii carry an inducible chromosomal AmpC β-lactamase. Under exposure to ceftriaxone (or another third-generation cephalosporin), derepressed mutants can emerge and cause clinical failure, even when the initial isolate tests susceptible. For serious infections such as bacteremia, IDSA guidance suggests cefepime (a poor AmpC inducer and stable to hydrolysis) when the MIC is ≤2. Carbapenems are reserved for cefepime MIC ≥4 (possible ESBL coproduction).

why_not.A: Ceftriaxone risks selecting AmpC-derepressed mutants during therapy for invasive infection; it's acceptable mainly for uncomplicated cystitis.
why_not.C: Piperacillin–tazobactam isn't suggested for serious AmpC-E infections (tazobactam is a weak AmpC inhibitor).
why_not.D: Effective, but unnecessarily broad when cefepime works; save carbapenems.
why_not.E: An aminoglycoside doesn't solve the AmpC derepression problem and adds toxicity.

questions.pearl: Serious infection with Enterobacter cloacae, K. aerogenes, or C. freundii → cefepime, not ceftriaxone, even if “susceptible.”
references: Tamma PD et al. IDSA 2024 Guidance on the Treatment of Antimicrobial-Resistant Gram-Negative Infections
questions.image_query: AmpC beta-lactamase induction derepression mechanism

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man who had a splenectomy after a car crash lives on Cape Cod and gardens daily. In July he develops 5 days of fever, fatigue, and dark urine, and now has dyspnea with bilateral infiltrates (SpO₂ 88% on 4 L). Hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, platelets 42,000/µL, LDH 1,280 U/L, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, bilirubin 3.6 mg/dL. A thin smear is shown; parasitemia is 12%.

diagrams.caption: Thin smear (schematic). Note the absence of pigment, pleomorphic rings, extracellular forms, and the four-part arrangement in one cell.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.C: Atovaquone and IV azithromycin plus red-cell exchange transfusion

questions.explanation: Intraerythrocytic rings without hemozoin pigment, extracellular merozoites, and a tetrad (“Maltese cross”) in an asplenic patient from New England in summer is Babesia microti. He has severe disease: parasitemia >10%, severe hemolysis, ARDS, and kidney injury. Treat with atovaquone plus IV azithromycin (or clindamycin plus quinine), and red-cell exchange transfusion is recommended for high-grade parasitemia (>10%) or severe hemolysis or organ dysfunction. Also test for Lyme and Anaplasma coinfection, since the same Ixodes tick transmits them.

why_not.A: Doxycycline treats Lyme and anaplasmosis coinfection but has no activity against Babesia.
why_not.B: Correct drugs, but omitting exchange transfusion in life-threatening disease with >10% parasitemia isn't recommended.
why_not.D: Artesunate is for malaria; it isn't standard for babesiosis.
why_not.E: An acceptable drug alternative, but it also omits exchange transfusion, and quinine is poorly tolerated.

questions.pearl: Babesia: no pigment, tetrads, asplenia, Northeast summer. Severe (parasitemia >10%, organ failure) → atovaquone + azithro AND exchange transfusion.
references: Krause PJ et al. IDSA/SHEA/AAN 2020 Babesiosis Guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2021
