questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has had intermittent jaundice since childhood, worse during viral illnesses. She had symptomatic gallstones at 22. Her mother had a splenectomy as a teenager. The spleen tip is palpable. Hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, MCV 86 fL, MCHC 37.8 g/dL (high), reticulocytes 8%, indirect bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL. Direct antiglobulin test is negative. The smear shows many small, dense red cells lacking central pallor.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lifelong extravascular hemolysis, an elevated MCHC, spherocytes, a negative DAT, splenomegaly, early pigment gallstones, and autosomal dominant inheritance (affected mother) indicate hereditary spherocytosis (defects in ankyrin, spectrin, or band 3). EMA-binding flow cytometry confirms atypical cases. Management: folate, and splenectomy for moderate-severe disease (often with cholecystectomy).

why_not.A: Warm AIHA also shows spherocytes, but the DAT is positive (IgG ± C3).
why_not.C: G6PD deficiency is X-linked with episodic oxidant hemolysis, bite cells, and Heinz bodies.
why_not.D: PK deficiency is autosomal recessive without spherocytes (echinocytes may be seen).
why_not.E: Thalassemia minor causes microcytosis with a normal or low MCHC and target cells.

questions.pearl: Spherocytes: DAT positive → AIHA; DAT negative + high MCHC + family history → hereditary spherocytosis.
references: Bolton-Maggs PHB et al. BSH Guideline on Hereditary Spherocytosis, Br J Haematol 2012
questions.image_query: hereditary spherocytosis peripheral smear spherocytes

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman taking dabigatran 150 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation (last dose 4 hours ago) presents with acute aphasia. CT shows a 22-mL left temporal intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Creatinine clearance is 45 mL/min. Thrombin time is markedly prolonged.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate reversal agent?
questions.explanation: Idarucizumab is a humanized antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with high affinity and reverses its effect within minutes (RE-VERSE AD). It is the specific reversal agent for direct thrombin inhibitor–associated life-threatening bleeding. If it's unavailable, PCC or aPCC are alternatives, and dabigatran is also dialyzable.

why_not.B: PCC is the fallback when idarucizumab isn't available, but it isn't specific.
why_not.C: FFP doesn't reverse a direct thrombin inhibitor and adds volume.
why_not.D: Andexanet is a decoy for factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban), not dabigatran.
why_not.E: Vitamin K reverses warfarin only.

questions.pearl: Dabigatran → idarucizumab. Xa inhibitors → andexanet or 4F-PCC. Warfarin → 4F-PCC + IV vitamin K.
references: Pollack CV et al. RE-VERSE AD, NEJM 2017
2022 AHA/ASA Spontaneous ICH Guideline
questions.image_query: intracerebral hemorrhage CT anticoagulant

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man is on postoperative day 7 after CABG. He has received subcutaneous unfractionated heparin since surgery. Platelets were 240,000/µL on day 3 and are 92,000/µL today. He now has left calf swelling, and duplex shows a new popliteal DVT. There is no sepsis, and no new drugs other than heparin.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.C: Stop all heparin, start argatroban (or another non-heparin anticoagulant), and send an anti-PF4/heparin immunoassay
options.E: Stop heparin and withhold anticoagulation until platelets recover

questions.explanation: A >50% platelet fall starting 5–10 days after heparin exposure, with new thrombosis and no other cause, gives a high 4Ts score. Management can't wait for confirmation: stop all heparin (including flushes) and start a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, or a DOAC in a stable patient), then send the anti-PF4 immunoassay with a functional assay if positive.

why_not.A: Warfarin alone in acute HIT depletes protein C and can cause venous limb gangrene; start it only after platelets recover, overlapping with a non-heparin agent.
why_not.B: LMWH cross-reacts with HIT antibodies and is contraindicated.
why_not.D: HIT is a prothrombotic, not hemorrhagic, disorder; platelet transfusion is reserved for bleeding or high-risk procedures.
why_not.E: Untreated HIT carries a very high thrombosis risk; he already has a DVT.

questions.pearl: High-probability HIT: stop heparin, start a non-heparin anticoagulant, then test. No warfarin until platelets recover; no LMWH; no routine platelets.
references: Cuker A et al. ASH 2018 Guidelines for HIT, Blood Adv 2018
questions.image_query: heparin induced thrombocytopenia mechanism PF4 antibody

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with JAK2 V617F–positive polycythemia vera had an ischemic stroke 2 years ago. He takes aspirin 81 mg daily and undergoes phlebotomy as needed; his hematocrit is 52% today. Platelets are 610,000/µL. He has pruritus after showers. He has no history of skin cancer.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his management?

options.C: Hydroxyurea, with phlebotomy to keep hematocrit <45%

questions.explanation: PV is high risk with age ≥60 or prior thrombosis (he has both). High-risk patients need cytoreduction in addition to low-dose aspirin and phlebotomy to a hematocrit <45% (CYTO-PV). Hydroxyurea is the standard first-line agent; ropeginterferon alfa-2b is an alternative.

why_not.A: Phlebotomy alone is for low-risk PV.
why_not.B: Ruxolitinib is second-line for hydroxyurea resistance or intolerance.
why_not.D: Anagrelide lowers platelets only and is used for essential thrombocythemia, not PV.
why_not.E: Adding warfarin to aspirin for arterial secondary prevention raises bleeding without proven benefit in PV.

questions.pearl: PV: everyone gets aspirin + Hct <45%. Age ≥60 or thrombosis → cytoreduce (hydroxyurea or interferon); ruxolitinib second line.
references: Marchioli R et al. CYTO-PV, NEJM 2013
NCCN Guidelines: Myeloproliferative Neoplasms 2025
questions.image_query: polycythemia vera plethora facial

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman with HFpEF and CKD receives 2 units of red cells, each over 2 hours, for a hemoglobin of 6.8 g/dL from a GI bleed. One hour after the second unit, she becomes acutely dyspneic. Temperature 37.0°C, BP 182/96 mmHg, HR 112/min, SpO₂ 84% on room air. JVP is elevated and there are diffuse crackles. Chest radiograph shows bilateral perihilar opacities, an enlarged cardiac silhouette, and new small effusions. NT-proBNP is 4,800 pg/mL (900 last month).
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Respiratory distress within 12 hours of transfusion with hypertension, elevated JVP, cardiomegaly, effusions, and a sharp rise in NT-proBNP in an older patient with heart failure and CKD is TACO, now the leading cause of transfusion-related death. Treat with oxygen, diuresis, and slower or smaller-volume transfusions in the future.

why_not.A: TRALI is noncardiogenic edema, often with hypotension and fever and a normal BNP and JVP; diuretics may worsen it.
why_not.B: Anaphylaxis brings hypotension, urticaria, angioedema, and bronchospasm (think IgA deficiency).
why_not.C: Acute hemolysis (ABO mismatch) causes fever, hypotension, flank pain, hemoglobinuria, and DIC.
why_not.E: Febrile non-hemolytic reactions cause fever and chills without hypoxemia.

questions.pearl: Post-transfusion dyspnea: hypertension + high BNP/JVP = TACO (diurese). Hypotension + fever + normal BNP = TRALI (support, no diuretics).
references: ISBT 2018 revised TACO surveillance definition
Semple JW et al. TRALI, Blood 2019
questions.image_query: TACO versus TRALI comparison table

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old woman has 3 days of fatigue and an episode of word-finding difficulty that resolved after 20 minutes. Temperature 37.6°C. Peripheral smear shows numerous schistocytes. Results are shown. ADAMTS13 activity has been sent; results will take 3 days.
TestResultReference
Hemoglobin8.1 g/dL12–16
Platelets12,000/µL150–400k
Reticulocytes7%0.5–2.5
LDH1,210 U/L<250
Indirect bilirubin2.6 mg/dL<0.9
Creatinine1.1 mg/dL0.5–1.0
PT/INR1.10.9–1.1
MCV88 fL80–100
DATNegative
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Start plasma exchange and glucocorticoids now
options.B: Await the ADAMTS13 result before treatment

questions.explanation: Microangiopathic hemolysis with severe thrombocytopenia, neurologic symptoms, and preserved renal function gives a PLASMIC score of 6–7 (high probability) for immune TTP, which is fatal in up to 90% of untreated patients. Don't wait for ADAMTS13: start plasma exchange and glucocorticoids immediately. Caplacizumab is added (ISTH) once TTP is likely, and rituximab is often given to suppress the anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibody.

why_not.B: Delaying treatment while waiting for the assay increases mortality.
why_not.C: Platelets may worsen microvascular thrombosis; give them only for life-threatening bleeding.
why_not.D: Complement inhibition is for complement-mediated (atypical) HUS, considered when ADAMTS13 is >10% and kidney injury is prominent.
why_not.E: IVIG has no established role in TTP.

questions.pearl: Suspected TTP (high PLASMIC score) → plasma exchange + steroids now ± caplacizumab; ADAMTS13 <10% confirms.
references: Zheng XL et al. ISTH Guidelines for TTP, J Thromb Haemost 2020
questions.image_query: schistocytes peripheral smear TTP

questions.stem:
A 72-year-old man with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate has worsening fatigue. He has no overt bleeding and takes no NSAIDs or anticoagulants. Results are shown. His last colonoscopy was 12 years ago.
TestResultReference
Hemoglobin9.8 g/dL13.5–17.5
MCV79 fL80–100
Ferritin85 ng/mL30–400
Transferrin saturation7%20–50%
Soluble transferrin receptorElevated
CRP38 mg/L<5
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Attribute the anemia to chronic inflammation; no further evaluation

questions.explanation: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant, so a ferritin of 85 ng/mL doesn't exclude iron deficiency during inflammation (thresholds of roughly 100 ng/mL are used when CRP is elevated). A TSAT of 7%, microcytosis, and an elevated soluble transferrin receptor (which, unlike ferritin, isn't raised by inflammation) indicate true iron deficiency superimposed on anemia of inflammation. In an older man, iron deficiency means GI blood loss until proven otherwise, so he needs bidirectional endoscopy.

why_not.A: Attributing everything to RA misses a possible GI malignancy.
why_not.B: ESAs don't address iron deficiency and aren't indicated here.
why_not.C: Marrow examination is rarely needed when serum markers and the clinical context are this clear.
why_not.E: Thalassemia trait doesn't lower TSAT or raise sTfR this way and wouldn't explain a new anemia.

questions.pearl: With inflammation, ferritin up to ~100 can still mean iron deficiency; low TSAT + high sTfR clinches it. Iron deficiency in a man or postmenopausal woman → scope.
references: Ko CW et al. AGA Clinical Practice Guidelines on Iron Deficiency Anemia, Gastroenterology 2020
Camaschella C. NEJM 2015 (iron-deficiency anemia)
questions.image_query: iron deficiency vs anemia of chronic disease lab comparison ferritin transferrin receptor

questions.stem:
A 32-year-old man has 3 weeks of abdominal pain and distension. Doppler ultrasound shows hepatic vein thrombosis with ascites. He notes dark urine on waking, which clears later in the day. Peripheral smear shows no schistocytes or spherocytes. Results are shown.
TestResultReference
Hemoglobin8.9 g/dL13.5–17.5
Reticulocytes6%0.5–2.5
WBC / ANC3,100 / 1,200 per µL
Platelets98,000/µL150–400k
LDH1,140 U/L<250
HaptoglobinUndetectable30–200
Direct antiglobulin testNegative
UrinalysisDipstick heme 3+, 0–2 RBC/hpf
questions.question: Which test is most likely to establish the underlying diagnosis?

options.B: Peripheral blood flow cytometry for GPI-anchored proteins (CD55/CD59, FLAER)

questions.explanation: Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis (undetectable haptoglobin, high LDH, hemoglobinuria that's worse in the morning), thrombosis at an unusual site (Budd–Chiari), and cytopenias form the triad of PNH. Loss of GPI-anchored complement regulators (CD55, CD59) leaves red cells exposed to complement. Diagnose with high-sensitivity flow cytometry (FLAER plus CD59 on granulocytes and monocytes). Treatment is a complement inhibitor (C5 or proximal) plus anticoagulation.

why_not.A: Myeloproliferative neoplasms are the most common cause of Budd–Chiari, but they cause cytosis, not Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis with cytopenias.
why_not.C: G6PD deficiency causes episodic oxidant-triggered hemolysis with bite cells, not thrombosis or marrow failure.
why_not.D: TTP has schistocytes and severe thrombocytopenia.
why_not.E: Hereditary spherocytosis causes extravascular hemolysis with spherocytes, and no thrombosis.

questions.pearl: Hemolysis + thrombosis (especially abdominal or cerebral veins) + cytopenias = PNH → flow cytometry (FLAER/CD59).
references: Brodsky RA. How I treat PNH, Blood 2021
Borowitz MJ et al. ICCS guidelines for PNH flow cytometry, Cytometry B 2010

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man of Mediterranean descent with newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma is about to start chemotherapy. As a child he had dark urine and severe anemia after eating fava beans. Today: uric acid 13.8 mg/dL, potassium 5.6 mEq/L, phosphate 5.9 mg/dL, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL (baseline 0.9). Urine output is adequate.
questions.question: Which of the following agents should be avoided in this patient?

options.D: Hemodialysis if hyperkalemia or uremia worsens despite medical therapy

questions.explanation: His childhood hemolysis after fava beans points to G6PD deficiency. Rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) converts uric acid to allantoin and generates hydrogen peroxide, causing severe hemolysis and methemoglobinemia in G6PD-deficient patients. It is contraindicated, and G6PD screening is recommended before use in at-risk populations. Manage TLS with aggressive hydration, allopurinol, phosphate binding, close electrolyte monitoring, and early dialysis if needed.

why_not.A: Hydration is the foundation of TLS prevention and treatment.
why_not.B: Allopurinol prevents further urate formation (it doesn't lower existing urate) and is safe in G6PD deficiency.
why_not.C: Phosphate binders help with hyperphosphatemia.
why_not.D: Dialysis is appropriate for refractory TLS complications.

questions.pearl: G6PD deficiency: no rasburicase (H₂O₂ → hemolysis and methemoglobinemia), and no methylene blue for its methemoglobinemia.
references: Cairo MS et al. TLS expert panel guidelines, Br J Haematol 2010
Rasburicase prescribing information (boxed warning)
questions.image_query: G6PD deficiency bite cells Heinz bodies smear

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with metastatic melanoma received his third cycle of ipilimumab plus nivolumab 2 weeks ago. He now has 8–10 watery stools daily above baseline, abdominal cramping, and nocturnal stools. Stool C. difficile and pathogen panels are negative. CT shows diffuse colonic wall thickening without perforation. He was started on IV methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg/day 72 hours ago, with no improvement.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Continue IV methylprednisolone for another 7 days before changing therapy
options.C: Resume nivolumab alone at a reduced dose

questions.explanation: This is grade 3 immune-mediated colitis (≥7 stools/day above baseline). Immunotherapy is held and high-dose steroids started. Steroid-refractory disease (no improvement within 48–72 hours) should get a selective immunosuppressant: infliximab or vedolizumab. Waiting longer increases the risk of perforation.

why_not.A: Prolonged ineffective steroids delay rescue and raise the risk of perforation and infection.
why_not.C: Rechallenge is considered only after resolution, and the combination isn't resumed after grade 3 colitis.
why_not.D: Surgery is for perforation, toxic megacolon, or failure of medical rescue.
why_not.E: Budesonide may help mild disease or serve as maintenance, not steroid-refractory grade 3 colitis.

questions.pearl: ICI colitis: grade ≥2 → steroids; no response in ~3 days → infliximab or vedolizumab.
references: Schneider BJ et al. ASCO Guideline: Management of irAEs, J Clin Oncol 2021
NCCN Management of Immunotherapy-Related Toxicities 2025
questions.image_query: immune checkpoint inhibitor colitis CT colonoscopy

questions.stem:
A 78-year-old man has a large, painful thigh hematoma after minimal trauma and extensive bruising on his arms. He has no prior bleeding history, including after a hip replacement 5 years ago, and takes no anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs. Hemoglobin has fallen from 13 to 8.4 g/dL. Coagulation studies are shown.
TestResultReference
PT / INR12.1 s / 1.0normal
aPTT78 s25–35
aPTT 1:1 mix, immediate38 s
aPTT 1:1 mix, after 2 h at 37°C66 s
Factor VIII activity2%50–150%
Bethesda inhibitor titer18 BU0
Lupus anticoagulant (dRVVT)Negative
Platelets / fibrinogenNormal
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.E: A bypassing agent (recombinant factor VIIa or aPCC) plus prednisone

questions.explanation: An isolated prolonged aPTT that initially corrects on mixing but prolongs again after incubation means a time-dependent inhibitor. Together with a low factor VIII, a high Bethesda titer, and new soft-tissue bleeding in an older adult, this is acquired hemophilia A (autoantibody against FVIII, associated with older age, malignancy, autoimmune disease, and the postpartum state). Treat bleeding with a bypassing agent (rFVIIa or aPCC; recombinant porcine FVIII is an alternative), and eradicate the inhibitor with immunosuppression (steroids ± cyclophosphamide or rituximab). Screen for an underlying cause.

why_not.A: Plasma provides too little FVIII and is neutralized by the inhibitor.
why_not.B: A high-titer inhibitor (18 BU) neutralizes human FVIII.
why_not.C: DDAVP releases endogenous FVIII, which is likewise neutralized; it's ineffective with high-titer inhibitors.
why_not.D: Cryoprecipitate's FVIII is also neutralized; it's mainly for fibrinogen replacement.

questions.pearl: Elderly + new soft-tissue bleeding + isolated long aPTT not corrected after incubation = acquired hemophilia A → bypass + immunosuppress.
references: Tiede A et al. International recommendations on acquired hemophilia A, Haematologica 2020
questions.image_query: acquired hemophilia A extensive ecchymoses soft tissue bleeding

questions.stem:
A 61-year-old man is evaluated for an IgG-κ monoclonal protein found during a workup for fatigue. Hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, calcium 9.4 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. Whole-body low-dose CT shows no lytic lesions, and whole-body MRI shows no focal lesions. Other results are shown.
TestResultReference
Serum M-protein (IgG-κ)2.1 g/dL
Bone marrow clonal plasma cells24%<10%
Serum free κ1,420 mg/L3.3–19.4
Serum free λ9 mg/L5.7–26.3
κ/λ ratio1580.26–1.65
questions.question: Which of the following best describes his condition?

options.C: High-risk smoldering myeloma; consider a clinical trial

questions.explanation: He has no CRAB features, but the 2014 IMWG criteria added three myeloma-defining biomarkers (“SLiM”), any one of which mandates treatment: Sixty percent or more clonal plasma cells, an involved/uninvolved Light-chain ratio ≥100 (with involved FLC ≥100 mg/L), or more than one focal lesion on MRI. His κ/λ ratio is ~158 with κ 1,420 mg/L, which meets the definition of active multiple myeloma.

why_not.A: MGUS requires <10% marrow plasma cells and an M-protein <3 g/dL with no myeloma-defining event.
why_not.B: Smoldering myeloma requires absence of all myeloma-defining events, including SLiM criteria.
why_not.C: High-risk smoldering (e.g., 20/2/20) would apply only if no SLiM criterion were met; here one is.
why_not.D: A solitary plasmacytoma is a single lesion with minimal or no marrow plasmacytosis.

questions.pearl: SLiM-CRAB: ≥60% plasma cells, FLC ratio ≥100 (involved ≥100 mg/L), >1 MRI focal lesion, or any CRAB → treat as myeloma.
references: Rajkumar SV et al. IMWG updated criteria, Lancet Oncol 2014
questions.image_query: multiple myeloma diagnostic criteria SLiM CRAB

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old man has 2 months of progressive numbness in his feet and hands, unsteady gait, and electric shocks down his spine when he flexes his neck. Friends note he keeps boxes of small metal cream chargers and balloons in his car. Exam: loss of vibration and position sense in the feet, positive Romberg sign, brisk knee reflexes with absent ankle jerks. Cervical MRI shows symmetric T2 hyperintensity in the dorsal columns. Results are shown.
TestResultReference
Hemoglobin / MCV12.8 g/dL / 102 fL
Serum vitamin B12340 pg/mL200–900
Methylmalonic acid1,240 nmol/L<400
Homocysteine48 µmol/L<15
Copper / zincNormal / normal
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Stop the exposure and give IM vitamin B12

questions.explanation: Recreational nitrous oxide (whippets) irreversibly oxidizes the cobalt in cobalamin, inactivating methionine synthase. This causes a functional B12 deficiency: serum B12 can be normal, but methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are elevated. The result is subacute combined degeneration (dorsal column and corticospinal) with peripheral neuropathy. Treatment is stopping N₂O and prompt parenteral B12; methionine supplementation is sometimes added.

why_not.B: Copper deficiency (after bariatric surgery or zinc excess) mimics this myelopathy, but MMA wouldn't be elevated and the exposure history points to N₂O.
why_not.C: Dorsal column lesions here are metabolic, not demyelinating MS; steroids won't help.
why_not.D: Folate alone may correct the anemia but can let the neurologic injury progress.
why_not.E: IVIG treats immune neuropathies like CIDP or GBS, not a metabolic myelopathy.

questions.pearl: Young person + dorsal column myelopathy + normal B12 but high MMA/homocysteine → nitrous oxide. Stop it; give IM B12.
references: Garakani A et al. Neurologic effects of recreational N₂O, Am J Addict 2016
Hathout L, El-Saden S. J Neurol Sci 2011

links.label: Wikipedia: Subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord

questions.image_query: subacute combined degeneration MRI inverted V sign dorsal columns

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old woman has 4 weeks of daily fevers to 39.6°C, each evening returning to normal by morning. An evanescent salmon-pink macular rash on her trunk appears with the fevers. She has sore throat, wrist and knee arthralgias, and splenomegaly. Repeated blood cultures, viral studies, and echocardiogram are negative. CT shows only mild lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly; bone marrow biopsy shows reactive changes without lymphoma. Results are shown.
TestResultReference
WBC22,400/µL (88% neutrophils)4.5–11
Ferritin12,400 ng/mL15–150
Glycosylated ferritin12%>50%
AST / ALT88 / 96 U/L<40
ANA / RFNegative / negative
ASO titerNormal
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Quotidian spiking fevers, an evanescent salmon-colored rash with the fevers, arthralgia, sore throat, neutrophilic leukocytosis, hepatitis, splenomegaly, and a markedly elevated ferritin with a low glycosylated fraction (<20%), after exclusion of infection and malignancy, is adult-onset Still disease (Yamaguchi criteria). Treat with glucocorticoids or IL-1/IL-6 blockade, and watch for macrophage activation syndrome.

why_not.A: SLE causes leukopenia, positive ANA, and low complement, not neutrophilia with ferritin >10,000.
why_not.C: Rheumatic fever requires evidence of preceding streptococcal infection with carditis or migratory arthritis and erythema marginatum.
why_not.D: DGI causes tenosynovitis and pustular lesions and usually positive cultures or NAAT.
why_not.E: Reactive arthritis follows enteric or GU infection with asymmetric oligoarthritis and enthesitis.

questions.pearl: Fever spikes + salmon rash + neutrophilia + ferritin >10,000 with low glycosylated ferritin = AOSD (after excluding infection and lymphoma).
references: Yamaguchi M et al. J Rheumatol 1992
Fautrel B et al. 2002 criteria
Feist E et al. Nat Rev Rheumatol 2018
questions.image_query: adult onset Still disease salmon rash

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has 6 weeks of symmetric polyarthralgias, low-grade fevers, and pleuritic chest pain with a small pericardial effusion. He has had resistant hypertension for several years, controlled for the past 2 years with hydralazine 100 mg three times daily added to other drugs. He has no rash, oral ulcers, cytopenias, or nephritis. ANA 1:640 (homogeneous); anti-histone antibodies positive; anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith negative; C3 and C4 normal; urinalysis normal.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Start prednisone and hydroxychloroquine and continue hydralazine
options.E: Discontinue hydralazine and substitute another antihypertensive

questions.explanation: A lupus-like illness with serositis and arthritis, anti-histone antibodies, no anti-dsDNA or anti-Smith, normal complements, and no renal or CNS disease, after prolonged high-dose hydralazine (a slow-acetylator risk), is drug-induced lupus. The key intervention is stopping the drug; symptoms usually resolve in weeks. NSAIDs or brief low-dose steroids help persistent serositis.

why_not.A: Continuing the culprit drug perpetuates the disease.
why_not.B: Mycophenolate is for organ-threatening SLE, such as lupus nephritis.
why_not.C: Belimumab is for active idiopathic SLE.
why_not.D: There's no evidence of nephritis (urinalysis is normal).

questions.pearl: Anti-histone +, dsDNA −, normal complement, no kidney involvement + hydralazine/procainamide/isoniazid/minocycline/anti-TNF → drug-induced lupus: stop the drug.
references: Rubin RL. Drug-induced lupus, Expert Opin Drug Saf 2015
questions.image_query: drug induced lupus vs systemic lupus antibodies comparison

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate 20 mg weekly was prescribed trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection 8 days ago. She now has painful oral ulcers and fever. WBC 1,200/µL (ANC 400), hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL, platelets 40,000/µL. Creatinine is 1.2 mg/dL (baseline 0.9).
questions.question: In addition to stopping both drugs and starting empiric antibiotics for neutropenic fever, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: TMP-SMX (an antifolate that also reduces methotrexate's renal clearance and displaces it from protein) can precipitate severe methotrexate toxicity even at low weekly doses: mucositis and pancytopenia. The antidote is leucovorin (folinic acid), which bypasses dihydrofolate reductase blockade. Folic acid can't, because it needs DHFR to become active.

why_not.A: Folic acid requires DHFR to become active, which methotrexate blocks.
why_not.C: Glucarpidase cleaves methotrexate for toxic levels after high-dose IV methotrexate with renal failure; it's not standard for low-dose oral toxicity.
why_not.D: Steroids don't reverse antifolate marrow toxicity.
why_not.E: Supportive transfusion may be needed, but it doesn't treat the toxicity.

questions.pearl: Low-dose methotrexate + TMP-SMX (or NSAIDs, PPIs, worsening CKD) → pancytopenia and mucositis → leucovorin.
references: Cudmore J et al. Methotrexate and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole toxicity, CMAJ 2014
ACR methotrexate safety guidance
questions.image_query: methotrexate toxicity mucositis oral ulcers

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman diagnosed with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis 11 months ago (anti-RNA polymerase III positive) started prednisone 30 mg daily 3 weeks ago for an inflammatory myopathy. She now has headache and blurred vision. BP 212/118 mmHg (previously 118/72). Creatinine 2.3 mg/dL (1.0 last month). Hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL with schistocytes; platelets 92,000/µL. Urinalysis shows 1+ protein and few cells.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.C: Captopril, uptitrated to normalize BP, and continued even if dialysis becomes necessary

questions.explanation: Abrupt malignant hypertension, rising creatinine, and microangiopathic hemolysis in early diffuse SSc with anti-RNA polymerase III, triggered by glucocorticoids ≥15 mg/day, is scleroderma renal crisis. ACE inhibitors transformed its prognosis: use rapidly titratable captopril to bring BP toward baseline over 72 hours, and continue it even if dialysis is required, because renal recovery can occur up to 2 years later.

why_not.A: Other antihypertensives can be added, but an ACE inhibitor is the cornerstone; labetalol alone isn't sufficient.
why_not.B: Plasma exchange isn't standard; the TMA here is driven by renal vascular injury.
why_not.D: Nitroprusside alone without ACE inhibition misses the disease-specific therapy.
why_not.E: More steroids are a risk factor for SRC and would worsen it.

questions.pearl: Early diffuse SSc + anti-RNA pol III + steroids ≥15 mg → watch BP. SRC = ACE inhibitor (captopril), even on dialysis.
references: Kowal-Bielecka O et al. EULAR SSc treatment recommendations, Ann Rheum Dis 2017
Lynch BM et al. UK SRC guidelines, Rheumatology 2016
questions.image_query: systemic sclerosis sclerodactyly skin thickening

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman has an unprovoked proximal DVT. Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG (80 GPL), and anti-β2-glycoprotein I IgG (72 U) are all positive and remain positive 12 weeks later. She has no SLE features. She would prefer a medication that doesn't need blood monitoring.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term anticoagulant?
questions.explanation: She has thrombotic APS with triple antiphospholipid positivity, the highest-risk profile. In TRAPS, rivaroxaban led to more arterial thromboses than warfarin in triple-positive patients, and guidelines recommend against DOACs in this setting. For a first venous event, warfarin with INR 2–3 (indefinitely) is standard.

why_not.A: Rivaroxaban was inferior (excess arterial events) in triple-positive APS.
why_not.B: Apixaban also failed to show noninferiority in APS (ASTRO-APS) and isn't recommended for triple positivity.
why_not.D: High-intensity warfarin didn't reduce recurrence after venous APS and increases bleeding.
why_not.E: Aspirin alone is inadequate secondary prevention after venous thrombosis in APS.

questions.pearl: Thrombotic APS, especially triple-positive: warfarin (INR 2–3), not DOACs.
references: Pengo V et al. TRAPS, Blood 2018
Tektonidou MG et al. EULAR 2019 APS recommendations
questions.image_query: antiphospholipid syndrome livedo reticularis

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man has 2 days of a hot, swollen right knee. He has had similar episodes in his wrist. Knee radiograph shows linear calcification of the meniscal cartilage. Synovial fluid: 24,000 WBC/µL (85% neutrophils), Gram stain negative. Polarized microscopy is shown.

diagrams.caption: Synovial fluid under compensated polarized light (schematic). Background magenta; arrow = slow axis of the red compensator.

questions.question: In addition to treating the acute arthritis, which of the following evaluations is most appropriate?

options.D: Ferritin and transferrin saturation, calcium/PTH, magnesium, and phosphate

questions.explanation: Short, rhomboid crystals that are blue when parallel to the compensator's slow axis (and yellow when perpendicular) are weakly positively birefringent: calcium pyrophosphate. Together with chondrocalcinosis, this is acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout). CPPD before age 60 should prompt a search for metabolic causes: hemochromatosis (also suggested by second and third MCP involvement), hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesemia (e.g., Gitelman syndrome), and hypophosphatasia (low ALP).

why_not.A: Urate is for gout; urate crystals are needle-shaped and yellow when parallel (negative birefringence).
why_not.B: HLA-B27 is relevant to spondyloarthritis, not crystal disease.
why_not.C: Anti-CCP is for rheumatoid arthritis, which isn't suggested by crystal-proven monoarthritis.
why_not.E: ANA isn't helpful here.

questions.pearl: CPP: rhomboid, weakly positive (Blue Parallel). MSU: needles, negative (Yellow Parallel). CPPD <60 → check iron, Ca/PTH, Mg, phosphate/ALP.
references: Rosenthal AK, Ryan LM. Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, NEJM 2016
Abhishek A et al. 2023 ACR/EULAR CPPD Classification Criteria
questions.image_query: calcium pyrophosphate crystals polarized light rhomboid positive birefringence

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman has 3 months of fatigue, low-grade fevers, and a 5-kg weight loss. Her left arm aches and tires when she brushes her hair. She has no headache, jaw claudication, or visual symptoms. BP is 148/80 mmHg in the right arm and 112/70 mmHg in the left; there's a left supraclavicular bruit. ESR 92 mm/h, CRP 64 mg/L. A left temporal artery biopsy (2.2 cm) shows no arteritis.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Imaging of the aorta and its branches (CTA, MRA, or FDG-PET)
options.B: Conclude that giant cell arteritis is excluded
options.E: Start aspirin and a statin for presumed atherosclerotic subclavian stenosis

questions.explanation: Systemic inflammation, arm claudication, inter-arm BP difference, and a subclavian bruit in a patient over 50 suggest large-vessel GCA. That subtype often spares the temporal arteries, so temporal artery biopsy is frequently negative. Confirm with vascular imaging of the aorta and its branches; FDG-PET also documents disease extent. Glucocorticoids (and often tocilizumab) are the treatment.

why_not.B: A negative TAB doesn't exclude large-vessel GCA, and the clinical picture is compelling.
why_not.C: Contralateral biopsy adds little yield in large-vessel disease without cranial symptoms.
why_not.D: Takayasu arteritis typically begins before age 40–50; at 68 this is GCA.
why_not.E: Atherosclerosis doesn't explain the fevers, weight loss, and ESR of 92.

questions.pearl: GCA without cranial symptoms (arm claudication, BP asymmetry, aortitis) → image the large vessels; TAB is often negative.
references: Maz M et al. 2021 ACR/VF Guideline for GCA and Takayasu Arteritis
Dejaco C et al. 2023 EULAR recommendations on imaging in LVV
questions.image_query: large vessel giant cell arteritis FDG PET aorta subclavian

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with SLE has taken hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily for 6 years with excellent disease control. She weighs 58 kg; eGFR is 88 and she takes no tamoxifen. She had a normal baseline eye exam but no retinal screening since then.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Continue the current dose and begin screening at 10 years of use
options.B: Reduce the dose to ≤5 mg/kg actual body weight per day and begin annual screening with SD-OCT and automated visual fields
options.E: Check hydroxychloroquine blood levels; no change in screening

questions.explanation: Retinopathy risk depends on daily dose relative to actual body weight and duration. The AAO recommends ≤5.0 mg/kg/day of real weight; for 58 kg that's ≤290 mg/day, so 400 mg is too high. Screening with SD-OCT plus automated visual fields is annual after 5 years of use (sooner with risk factors such as renal disease or tamoxifen). HCQ reduces SLE flares, organ damage, thrombosis, and mortality, so it should be continued at a safe dose.

why_not.A: Her dose is excessive, and annual screening should already have begun at 5 years.
why_not.C: Stopping HCQ increases the risk of lupus flares; dose adjustment and screening manage the retinal risk.
why_not.D: Chloroquine is more retinotoxic.
why_not.E: Blood levels help assess adherence but don't replace weight-based dosing and retinal screening.

questions.pearl: HCQ ≤5 mg/kg actual weight; baseline exam, then annual SD-OCT + visual fields after 5 years. Don't stop it in SLE.
references: Marmor MF et al. AAO Recommendations on Screening for Chloroquine and Hydroxychloroquine Retinopathy, Ophthalmology 2016
Rosenbaum JT et al. AAO/ACR/AAD/RDS Joint Statement on HCQ 2021
questions.image_query: hydroxychloroquine retinopathy bull's eye maculopathy OCT

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man of Korean descent has had 4 gout flares in the past year and has a tophus on his right olecranon. eGFR is 45 mL/min/1.73 m². Serum urate is 9.4 mg/dL. He has no history of drug rashes. You plan urate-lowering therapy.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Start febuxostat 80 mg daily as first-line therapy
options.C: Test for HLA-B*58:01 before starting allopurinol

questions.explanation: HLA-B*58:01 strongly predicts allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS or SJS/TEN, which can be fatal); the allele is common in people of Korean, Han Chinese, and Thai descent, and in African American patients. ACR recommends testing before starting allopurinol in these groups. If negative, start allopurinol at a low dose (≤100 mg/day, lower in CKD) and titrate to urate <6 mg/dL with flare prophylaxis. If positive, use an alternative such as febuxostat.

why_not.A: Starting at 300 mg in CKD increases hypersensitivity risk, and HLA status is unknown.
why_not.B: ACR prefers allopurinol as first-line ULT, including in moderate-severe CKD; febuxostat is the alternative.
why_not.D: Uricosurics are less effective with reduced eGFR and raise the risk of stones.
why_not.E: Pegloticase is for refractory gout after oral ULT fails.

questions.pearl: Allopurinol: start low, go slow. Test HLA-B*58:01 first in Southeast Asian ancestry (Han Chinese, Korean, Thai) and African American patients.
references: FitzGerald JD et al. 2020 ACR Guideline for the Management of Gout, Arthritis Care Res 2020
questions.image_query: gout tophus olecranon

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man has 3 years of slowly progressive weakness. He has trouble gripping his golf club and climbing stairs, and recently started choking on solids. Exam shows asymmetric weakness and atrophy of the finger flexors (worse on the left) and quadriceps, with relatively preserved deltoids. There's no rash. Reflexes are normal and there are no upper motor neuron signs. CK is 650 U/L. EMG shows a mixed myopathic pattern with fibrillations. A 6-month trial of prednisone 60 mg daily produced no improvement.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An older man with slowly progressive, asymmetric weakness of finger flexors and quadriceps, dysphagia, a mildly elevated CK, and no response to glucocorticoids has inclusion body myositis. Biopsy shows endomysial inflammation with rimmed vacuoles and protein aggregates; anti-cN1A antibodies support it. No immunosuppressant has proven benefit; management is exercise, physical therapy, and dysphagia care.

why_not.A: Polymyositis is symmetric and proximal, responds to steroids, and is now a diagnosis of exclusion often reclassified as IBM.
why_not.B: Dermatomyositis has characteristic skin findings and proximal symmetric weakness.
why_not.C: IMNM causes subacute, severe proximal weakness with a very high CK (often >5,000) and anti-HMGCR antibodies.
why_not.E: ALS combines upper and lower motor neuron signs with a normal or minimally elevated CK.

questions.pearl: Older man + finger flexor and quadriceps weakness + dysphagia + steroid failure = IBM. Rimmed vacuoles; anti-cN1A.
references: Greenberg SA. Inclusion body myositis, Nat Rev Rheumatol 2019
ENMC IBM research diagnostic criteria 2011
questions.image_query: inclusion body myositis rimmed vacuoles biopsy

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has painless jaundice and a 4-kg weight loss. CT shows a diffusely enlarged “sausage-shaped” pancreas with a low-attenuation peripheral rim and no discrete mass; there's also a smooth hilar bile duct stricture. Both submandibular glands are firm and enlarged. Serum IgG4 is 480 mg/dL (reference <135). CA 19-9 is mildly elevated. EUS-guided core biopsy shows dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, and >50 IgG4-positive plasma cells per high-power field, without malignancy.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.D: Biliary stenting alone without systemic therapy

questions.explanation: Multi-organ involvement (type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis, IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis, submandibular sialadenitis), elevated serum IgG4, and the classic histology (storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, abundant IgG4+ plasma cells) establish IgG4-related disease. Glucocorticoids produce a rapid, dramatic response, which also supports the diagnosis. Relapses are common; rituximab or inebilizumab (approved 2025) are used for maintenance or relapse.

why_not.A: Resection of a steroid-responsive inflammatory mass is a classic, avoidable error once malignancy is excluded.
why_not.B: Ursodiol is for PBC; it doesn't treat IgG4-related cholangitis.
why_not.C: Biopsy excluded adenocarcinoma.
why_not.D: A stent may be needed temporarily for jaundice, but it doesn't treat the inflammatory disease.

questions.pearl: Sausage pancreas + hilar stricture + salivary gland swelling + high IgG4 + storiform fibrosis → steroids (exclude cancer first).
references: Wallace ZS et al. 2019 ACR/EULAR IgG4-RD Classification Criteria
Khosroshahi A et al. International consensus on IgG4-RD management, Arthritis Rheumatol 2015
Stone JH et al. MITIGATE, NEJM 2025
questions.image_query: autoimmune pancreatitis sausage shaped pancreas CT capsule-like rim

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with SLE and class IV lupus nephritis, in complete renal remission for 14 months on mycophenolate mofetil 1 g twice daily, hydroxychloroquine, and prednisone 5 mg daily, wants to conceive. She is anti-Ro/SSA positive, and antiphospholipid antibodies are negative. BP is 118/74 mmHg; urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 0.1 g/g.
questions.question: Which medication change is most appropriate before she attempts conception?

options.D: Switch mycophenolate to azathioprine and confirm stable disease for at least 6 weeks before conception

questions.explanation: Mycophenolate is teratogenic (embryopathy and miscarriage) and should be stopped at least 6 weeks before conception, replaced with a pregnancy-compatible agent such as azathioprine (or tacrolimus), with disease stability confirmed before trying. Hydroxychloroquine should continue: it lowers flare risk and, in anti-Ro–positive women, reduces the risk of congenital heart block. Low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks (preeclampsia prophylaxis) and fetal echo surveillance between weeks 16 and 26 are also recommended.

why_not.A: Stopping HCQ increases flares and removes protection against neonatal heart block.
why_not.B: Methotrexate is also teratogenic and must be stopped 1–3 months before conception.
why_not.C: Stopping everything risks a nephritis flare, which is dangerous in pregnancy.
why_not.E: She's aPL-negative with no thrombosis history; warfarin is teratogenic.

questions.pearl: Planning pregnancy in SLE: MMF → azathioprine ≥6 weeks before conception; keep HCQ; add aspirin; anti-Ro → fetal heart monitoring.
references: Sammaritano LR et al. 2020 ACR Guideline for Reproductive Health in Rheumatic Diseases
questions.image_query: neonatal lupus congenital heart block anti-Ro

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman has 6 weeks of rash and 4 weeks of rapidly worsening dyspnea. She has violaceous papules over her knuckles, painful red papules on her palmar creases, and punched-out ulcers over her finger pads and elbows. Muscle strength is nearly normal; CK is 140 U/L. Ferritin is 1,850 ng/mL. HRCT shows lower-lobe peribronchovascular consolidation and ground-glass opacities that progressed markedly over 3 weeks.
questions.question: Which autoantibody is most likely positive?
questions.explanation: Clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis with painful palmar papules, cutaneous ulcers, high ferritin, and rapidly progressive ILD is the signature of anti-MDA5 (melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5) dermatomyositis, which carries high early mortality from respiratory failure. It warrants immediate aggressive combination immunosuppression (high-dose glucocorticoids plus a calcineurin inhibitor plus cyclophosphamide or tofacitinib, ± plasma exchange).

why_not.B: Anti-Jo-1 (antisynthetase syndrome) causes ILD with myositis, mechanic's hands, arthritis, and Raynaud's, but typically with clear myositis and a high CK.
why_not.C: Anti-TIF1-γ is associated with cancer-associated dermatomyositis and extensive skin disease, usually without ILD.
why_not.D: Anti-Mi-2 causes classic DM with prominent skin and muscle disease, a good steroid response, and low ILD risk.
why_not.E: Anti-SRP causes severe necrotizing myopathy with a very high CK and no rash.

questions.pearl: DM with little or no myositis + palmar papules + skin ulcers + high ferritin + rapidly progressive ILD → anti-MDA5 (emergency).
references: Lundberg IE et al. Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021
Romero-Bueno F et al. Semin Arthritis Rheum 2020
questions.image_query: anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis palmar papules digital ulcers

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with hypertension and atrial fibrillation (off anticoagulation for 2 weeks after a dental extraction) noticed drooping of the right side of his mouth 40 minutes ago. He can wrinkle both sides of his forehead and close both eyes tightly. His speech is slightly slurred, and his right hand feels clumsy.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Prednisone 60 mg daily for presumed Bell palsy
options.D: MRI of the internal auditory canals in 2 weeks
options.E: Activate the stroke pathway with emergent noncontrast CT and CT angiography

questions.explanation: Lower facial weakness that spares the forehead means an upper motor neuron (central) lesion: the upper face gets bilateral cortical input. Together with dysarthria, hand clumsiness, sudden onset, and interrupted anticoagulation for AF, this is an acute stroke (perhaps a dysarthria–clumsy hand syndrome or a cortical branch embolus). It needs immediate imaging for thrombolysis or thrombectomy decisions.

why_not.A: Bell palsy (peripheral, LMN) involves the forehead and doesn't cause dysarthria or limb clumsiness.
why_not.B: Antivirals and steroids are for Bell palsy, which this isn't.
why_not.C: Lyme facial palsy is peripheral, with forehead involvement.
why_not.D: A delayed IAC study is for peripheral palsy with hearing loss or atypical course; this is time-critical.

questions.pearl: Forehead spared = central (stroke) → code stroke. Forehead involved = peripheral (Bell, Lyme, Ramsay Hunt).
references: Baugh RF et al. AAO-HNS Bell's Palsy Guideline 2013
2019 AHA/ASA Acute Ischemic Stroke Guideline
questions.image_query: central versus peripheral facial palsy forehead sparing diagram

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman developed anxiety, insomnia, and paranoid delusions 3 weeks ago and was admitted to psychiatry. She then had two seizures, followed by decreased responsiveness, repetitive orofacial movements, and fluctuating BP and heart rate. CSF shows 42 lymphocytes/µL with normal glucose; HSV PCR is negative. EEG shows generalized slowing with an extreme delta brush pattern. MRI brain is normal. CSF anti-NMDA receptor (GluN1) antibodies are pending; IV methylprednisolone and IVIG have been started.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most important additional evaluation?

options.B: Chest CT for small cell lung cancer
options.D: Repeat HSV PCR in 1 week before any further workup

questions.explanation: Psychiatric onset progressing to seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic instability, and decreased consciousness, with lymphocytic CSF and extreme delta brush, is classic anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. In young women it's frequently paraneoplastic from an ovarian teratoma, so pelvic MRI and ultrasound are essential. Tumor removal plus immunotherapy improves outcomes and lowers relapse risk.

why_not.A: Biopsy is unnecessary; diagnosis is clinical plus CSF antibodies.
why_not.B: SCLC is associated with anti-Hu and other syndromes in older smokers, not NMDAR encephalitis in young women.
why_not.D: HSV can trigger NMDAR encephalitis, but HSV PCR is negative and tumor screening shouldn't wait.
why_not.E: Testicular germ cell tumors are relevant in men (e.g., anti-Ma2, anti-KLHL11).

questions.pearl: Young woman + psychosis → seizures, dyskinesias, dysautonomia → anti-NMDAR → look for ovarian teratoma and remove it.
references: Dalmau J et al. Lancet Neurol 2019 (anti-NMDAR encephalitis review)
Graus F et al. Clinical approach to autoimmune encephalitis, Lancet Neurol 2016
questions.image_query: extreme delta brush EEG anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man is hospitalized for pneumonia. His wife reports 2 years of well-formed visual hallucinations of children in the house, days of marked confusion alternating with near-normal days, and years of shouting and punching in his sleep. He has mild rigidity and bradykinesia. Tonight he is agitated and frightened by hallucinations, and the cross-cover physician is considering medication.
questions.question: Which of the following medications should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, and parkinsonism are the core features of dementia with Lewy bodies. Up to 50% of patients have severe neuroleptic sensitivity: typical antipsychotics like haloperidol can cause abrupt, sometimes irreversible worsening of parkinsonism, confusion, autonomic failure, NMS-like reactions, and death. Non-drug measures come first; cholinesterase inhibitors help hallucinations, and if an antipsychotic is unavoidable, low-dose quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin are used.

why_not.A: Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line for cognitive and psychotic symptoms in DLB.
why_not.C: Low-dose quetiapine is a relatively safe choice when an antipsychotic is needed.
why_not.D: Melatonin is safe and helps REM sleep behavior disorder.
why_not.E: A 5-HT2A inverse agonist without D2 blockade, approved for Parkinson disease psychosis.

questions.pearl: DLB = hallucinations + fluctuations + RBD + parkinsonism → no haloperidol (neuroleptic sensitivity).
references: McKeith IG et al. Fourth DLB Consortium criteria, Neurology 2017
Taylor JP et al. Lancet Neurol 2020
questions.image_query: dementia with Lewy bodies DaTscan reduced uptake

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man had bloody diarrhea 3 weeks ago. Over 5 days he has developed ascending leg weakness, now with difficulty standing and hand weakness. Reflexes are absent throughout. CSF: protein 148 mg/dL, 2 white cells/µL. Nerve conduction studies show reduced motor amplitudes. FVC is 32 mL/kg and stable; he is admitted to a monitored unit.
questions.question: Which disease-modifying therapy is most appropriate?

options.D: Plasma exchange followed immediately by IVIG

questions.explanation: Post-infectious (likely Campylobacter) acute ascending flaccid weakness with areflexia and albuminocytologic dissociation is Guillain–Barré syndrome, probably the axonal variant (AMAN) given the low motor amplitudes. IVIG (or plasma exchange) started within 2–4 weeks hastens recovery when the patient can't walk unaided. Monitor FVC and NIF closely, along with dysautonomia.

why_not.A: Glucocorticoids don't help GBS, and oral steroids may delay recovery.
why_not.B: Adding methylprednisolone to IVIG gives no significant additional benefit.
why_not.D: Sequential PLEX then IVIG wasn't better than either alone, and PLEX would wash out the IVIG.
why_not.E: Rituximab has no role in GBS.

questions.pearl: GBS: IVIG or PLEX (equivalent, not combined, no steroids). Intubate by the 20/30/40 rule (FVC <20 mL/kg, NIF > −30, MEP <40).
references: van Doorn PA et al. EAN/PNS Guideline on GBS, Eur J Neurol 2023
questions.image_query: Guillain-Barre syndrome nerve conduction albuminocytologic dissociation

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman was last seen well 15 hours ago and was found with left hemiplegia, gaze deviation, and neglect (NIHSS 18). Her baseline modified Rankin score is 0. CT shows no hemorrhage. CTA shows a right M1 occlusion. CT perfusion: ischemic core 20 mL, hypoperfused tissue (Tmax >6 s) 110 mL.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.B: No reperfusion therapy; she is outside the treatment window
options.E: Repeat imaging in 24 hours to reassess

questions.explanation: With a proximal anterior circulation LVO, a small core and a large perfusion mismatch (ratio >1.8, mismatch volume ≥15 mL), she meets DEFUSE 3 criteria (6–16 hours); DAWN extends selection to 24 hours with clinical–core mismatch. Thrombectomy dramatically improves functional independence (NNT ≈ 2–3).

why_not.A: IV thrombolysis at 15 hours isn't standard, and lysis alone rarely recanalizes an M1 occlusion.
why_not.B: Tissue-based imaging selection extends thrombectomy eligibility to 24 hours.
why_not.C: Anticoagulation isn't acute stroke therapy.
why_not.E: Delay converts penumbra to infarct.

questions.pearl: LVO at 6–24 h with a small core and big penumbra (DEFUSE 3/DAWN) → thrombectomy.
references: Albers GW et al. DEFUSE 3, NEJM 2018
Nogueira RG et al. DAWN, NEJM 2018
questions.image_query: CT perfusion core penumbra mismatch map stroke

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man has 1 year of a slow, broad-based, shuffling gait in which his feet seem stuck to the floor, urinary urgency with incontinence, and slowed thinking. There's no rest tremor, and arm swing is relatively preserved. MRI shows ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy, with tight high-convexity sulci and dilated Sylvian fissures.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: High-volume lumbar puncture (tap test) with gait assessment before and after

questions.explanation: Gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, and cognitive slowing, with disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus (DESH) on MRI, suggest normal pressure hydrocephalus. A high-volume LP (30–50 mL) with objective gait testing (e.g., timed up-and-go, 10-m walk) predicts shunt response. Improvement supports VP shunting; extended lumbar drainage is used if the tap test is equivocal.

why_not.B: Cholinesterase inhibitors don't treat NPH, and gait predominance argues against Alzheimer disease.
why_not.C: Levodopa doesn't help NPH; the parkinsonism here is lower-body without tremor.
why_not.D: Shunting without a supportive tap test exposes non-responders to surgical risk.
why_not.E: Lumbar stenosis can affect gait but doesn't explain the triad or the MRI findings.

questions.pearl: Wet, wobbly, wacky + DESH on MRI → tap test (30–50 mL) → shunt if gait improves.
references: Nakajima M et al. Japanese Guidelines for iNPH 3rd ed., Neurol Med Chir 2021
Williams MA, Malm J. Continuum 2016
questions.image_query: normal pressure hydrocephalus MRI DESH callosal angle

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with no prior seizures is brought in having had a generalized convulsion that began 12 minutes ago. She received IV lorazepam 4 mg on arrival and again 5 minutes later, but is still convulsing. Airway is supported; glucose is 104 mg/dL; pregnancy test is negative.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next medication?

options.A: A third dose of IV lorazepam
options.B: Propofol infusion as the next agent

questions.explanation: Seizures continuing despite adequate benzodiazepine doses is established status epilepticus, requiring a second-line IV antiseizure drug. In ESETT, levetiracetam (60 mg/kg), fosphenytoin (20 mg PE/kg), and valproate (40 mg/kg) were equally effective (~50% cessation). Levetiracetam is often chosen for its safety: no hypotension or arrhythmia (unlike fosphenytoin) and no teratogenicity concerns in someone of childbearing potential (unlike valproate). If seizures continue, move to anesthetic infusions (refractory SE).

why_not.A: More benzodiazepine beyond two adequate doses adds respiratory depression with little benefit.
why_not.B: Anesthetic infusions are third-line, for refractory SE after a second-line agent fails.
why_not.C: Enteral administration is too slow for status epilepticus.
why_not.E: Rectal diazepam is for prehospital use without IV access, and she has already had benzodiazepines.

questions.pearl: SE: benzo → (if still seizing) levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate (ESETT: equal) → anesthetic infusion.
references: Kapur J et al. ESETT, NEJM 2019
Glauser T et al. AES Guideline for Convulsive Status Epilepticus, Epilepsy Curr 2016
questions.image_query: status epilepticus treatment algorithm timeline

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman has sudden right hemianopia and confusion. CT shows a 25-mL left parieto-occipital lobar hemorrhage. She has well-controlled hypertension and takes no antithrombotics. Platelets and coagulation studies are normal. MRI with susceptibility-weighted imaging shows multiple strictly lobar cortical–subcortical microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis over both convexities, with no microbleeds in the basal ganglia, thalami, or brainstem. CTA shows no vascular malformation.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of the hemorrhage?

options.C: Hemorrhagic transformation of an ischemic stroke

questions.explanation: A lobar ICH in an older adult with strictly lobar microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis meets the Boston criteria v2.0 for probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy (β-amyloid deposition in cortical and leptomeningeal vessels). CAA carries a high risk of recurrent lobar ICH, which affects later decisions about antithrombotic therapy (e.g., favoring left atrial appendage occlusion over anticoagulation if AF develops).

why_not.A: Hypertensive ICH involves deep structures (putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum) with deep microbleeds.
why_not.B: CTA shows no AVM, and AVMs typically cause hemorrhage in younger patients.
why_not.C: There was no preceding ischemic infarct, and the microbleed pattern points elsewhere.
why_not.E: Cavernomas show a “popcorn” lesion with a hemosiderin rim, not diffuse lobar microbleeds and siderosis.

questions.pearl: Lobar ICH + strictly lobar microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis in an older adult = CAA (Boston 2.0).
references: Charidimou A et al. Boston Criteria v2.0 for CAA, Lancet Neurol 2022
2022 AHA/ASA Spontaneous ICH Guideline

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with AChR-antibody–positive myasthenia gravis, stable on pyridostigmine, was started on levofloxacin for community-acquired pneumonia 2 days ago. She now has worsening ptosis, nasal speech, difficulty swallowing secretions, and dyspnea. She can count to only 12 in one breath. Forced vital capacity is 1.1 L (17 mL/kg), down from 2.0 L yesterday; negative inspiratory force is −22 cm H₂O. ABG: pH 7.38, PaCO₂ 42 mmHg.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.B: High-dose prednisone as the sole treatment
options.C: Observe on the ward and repeat FVC in the morning
options.D: Switch levofloxacin to azithromycin and continue current care
options.E: ICU admission with elective intubation, stopping levofloxacin, and IVIG or plasma exchange

questions.explanation: This is impending myasthenic crisis precipitated by a fluoroquinolone. Bedside thresholds (FVC <20 mL/kg, NIF weaker than −30 cm H₂O, or a rapid decline) and bulbar weakness call for elective intubation before hypercapnia develops; a normal PaCO₂ is a late and falsely reassuring finding. Stop the offending drug and give rapid therapy: plasma exchange or IVIG. Pyridostigmine is usually held while intubated to reduce secretions.

why_not.A: More pyridostigmine increases secretions and risks a cholinergic crisis.
why_not.B: High-dose steroids alone can cause transient worsening and act too slowly.
why_not.C: Rapidly falling FVC with bulbar weakness can precede sudden respiratory arrest.
why_not.D: Macrolides (azithromycin) can also exacerbate MG, and this ignores the respiratory emergency.

questions.pearl: MG crisis: FVC <20, NIF weaker than −30 → intubate electively; PLEX or IVIG; stop fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides, magnesium.
references: Narayanaswami P et al. International Consensus Guidance for MG, 2020 update, Neurology 2021

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman (BMI 36 kg/m²) has 3 weeks of daily headache that's worse lying down, pulsatile whooshing in her ears, and brief episodes of visual dimming when she stands. She started a combined oral contraceptive 2 months ago. Exam: bilateral papilledema and a left abducens palsy; otherwise normal. Brain MRI without contrast shows a partially empty sella and flattened posterior globes, with no mass or hydrocephalus.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Lumbar puncture with opening pressure, then acetazolamide

questions.explanation: Her features fit idiopathic intracranial hypertension, but IIH is a diagnosis of exclusion. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis produces an identical picture, and her estrogen exposure raises that risk. MR venography (or CT venography) must come before attributing papilledema to IIH; finding CVT would change treatment to anticoagulation. LP with opening pressure and CSF analysis follows.

why_not.A: LP will be needed, but treating as IIH before excluding venous sinus thrombosis risks missing CVT.
why_not.C: Topiramate is a second-line IIH therapy; the diagnosis isn't established yet.
why_not.D: Surgery is for fulminant or refractory vision loss after diagnosis.
why_not.E: Papilledema threatens vision and needs a diagnosis and treatment.

questions.pearl: Papilledema with normal parenchymal MRI → venography before calling it IIH (especially with estrogen, pregnancy, or thrombophilia).
references: Mollan SP et al. IIH consensus guidelines, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2018
Saposnik G et al. AHA Scientific Statement on CVT 2024
questions.image_query: papilledema fundus photograph

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man went to bed normal at 11 PM and woke at 6:30 AM with right hemiparesis and aphasia (NIHSS 12). He arrives at 7:15 AM. Glucose 128 mg/dL, BP 168/92 mmHg. He takes no anticoagulants. Noncontrast CT shows no hemorrhage or early ischemic change; CT angiography shows no large-vessel occlusion. MRI is immediately available.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: No thrombolysis, because time since last known well exceeds 4.5 hours
options.E: Brain MRI to look for a DWI–FLAIR mismatch to guide IV thrombolysis

questions.explanation: Last known well is >4.5 hours ago, but the stroke may have begun shortly before waking. A DWI lesion without corresponding FLAIR hyperintensity (DWI–FLAIR mismatch) indicates the infarct is likely <4.5 hours old. In WAKE-UP, IV alteplase selected this way improved functional outcome, and guidelines endorse IV thrombolysis for unknown-onset stroke with DWI–FLAIR mismatch (DWI lesion < ⅓ of the MCA territory). Perfusion-mismatch selection (EXTEND) is an alternative.

why_not.A: The clock-based cutoff ignores tissue-based selection for unknown-onset stroke.
why_not.B: Aspirin should be withheld for 24 hours if thrombolysis is given, and giving it now forecloses a more effective therapy.
why_not.C: No large-vessel occlusion is seen, so there's no target for thrombectomy.
why_not.D: Acute heparin doesn't improve outcomes and increases hemorrhage.

questions.pearl: Wake-up stroke: DWI+/FLAIR− mismatch (or perfusion mismatch) → IV thrombolysis is reasonable.
references: Thomalla G et al. WAKE-UP, NEJM 2018
Powers WJ et al. 2019 AHA/ASA Acute Ischemic Stroke Guideline Update

A 56-year-old woman had Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 10 years ago. She has 8 months of progressive gait unsteadiness and numb feet. She uses several tubes of denture adhesive a week. Exam: spastic gait, brisk knee reflexes, extensor plantar responses, loss of vibration and position sense in the legs, positive Romberg sign. MRI shows T2 hyperintensity in the dorsal columns of the cervical cord. Results are shown.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Stop the zinc-containing adhesive and start copper supplementation

questions.explanation: A subacute combined degeneration–like myeloneuropathy with normal B12 and MMA, plus anemia and neutropenia, points to copper deficiency. She has two causes: malabsorption after gastric bypass and excess zinc from denture cream. Zinc induces enterocyte metallothionein, which traps copper. Treatment is removing the zinc source and copper repletion; hematologic abnormalities recover, but neurologic deficits often only stabilize.

why_not.B: B12 and MMA are normal; B12 won't help.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman, 10 days postpartum, has had five sudden, explosive headaches over 8 days, each peaking within seconds, two of them during bowel movements. She takes sertraline and has been using pseudoephedrine for congestion. BP 152/88 mmHg; neurologic exam is normal. Noncontrast CT shows a small amount of subarachnoid blood in a right frontal convexity sulcus; CSF white-cell count and protein are normal. CTA shows multifocal segmental narrowing and dilation of branches of the MCA and ACA bilaterally, without aneurysm.
questions.question: Which of the following should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Recurrent thunderclap headaches triggered by Valsalva, in the postpartum period with serotonergic and sympathomimetic drugs, plus a convexity SAH and a “string of beads” vasoconstriction on angiography, is RCVS. It's often confused with primary angiitis of the CNS, but glucocorticoids are associated with worse outcomes in RCVS and should be avoided. Management is removing triggers, avoiding vasoconstrictors (including triptans), analgesia, BP control, and often a calcium-channel blocker (nimodipine or verapamil). Vasoconstriction resolves within ~3 months.

why_not.A: Removing vasoactive triggers is a key step.
why_not.B: Nimodipine is commonly used and may reduce headache frequency.
why_not.D: Simple analgesia is appropriate; avoid triptans and ergots.
why_not.E: Valsalva is a common trigger, so preventing it helps.

questions.pearl: Recurrent thunderclaps + convexity SAH + beaded arteries (postpartum or on SSRIs/decongestants) = RCVS. No steroids, no triptans; it resolves in about 3 months.
references: Singhal AB et al. Glucocorticoid-associated worsening in RCVS, Neurology 2017
Ducros A. Lancet Neurol 2012

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man from central Virginia has had three episodes of generalized hives, abdominal cramping, and light-headedness that woke him around 2 AM. Each followed a hamburger or steak dinner about 5 hours earlier; he has eaten chicken and fish without problems. He hikes frequently and has had many tick bites, including from ticks with a single white spot on the back. Baseline tryptase is normal.
questions.question: Which of the following tests is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

options.A: Skin prick test with commercial beef extract

questions.explanation: Delayed (3–6 hour) anaphylaxis after mammalian meat, often at night, in someone with lone star tick bites (single white dot) is α-gal syndrome: IgE against galactose-α-1,3-galactose, induced by tick bites. Confirm with α-gal–specific IgE. Management is avoiding mammalian meat (and sometimes dairy or gelatin), carrying epinephrine, and avoiding further tick bites. The same IgE explains immediate reactions to cetuximab.

why_not.A: Commercial meat skin-prick extracts are insensitive for α-gal.
why_not.C: Peanut allergy causes immediate reactions after peanut, not delayed reactions after red meat.
why_not.D: Carcinoid causes flushing and diarrhea unrelated to specific meals or hives.
why_not.E: Bradykinin angioedema doesn't cause urticaria.

questions.pearl: Hives or anaphylaxis 3–6 h after red meat + lone star tick bites = α-gal syndrome (also cetuximab reactions).
references: Commins SP. α-Gal syndrome, J Allergy Clin Immunol Pract 2020
CDC Alpha-gal Syndrome Clinical Guidance 2023
